question: What are the default size limits for file uploads and total request size for the new multipart upload support on the OpenAI-compatible API endpoints?

evidence.title: multipart: add per-part/file size guards, content-type validation, and OpenAI-compat field mapping
evidence.text:
description:
Motivation: customers using the OpenAI-compatibility layer and the tool/function-calling endpoints were able to upload large multipart payloads and malformed parts which caused OOMs and destabilized streaming. This PR centralizes multipart validation into the API gateway handler and adds explicit per-part and total payload limits, content-type sniffing, and dual-field support for OpenAI-compat clients (accept both 'file' and 'files' form fields). The change is intentionally conservative: we validate before handing off to the streaming runtime so we can guarantee early rejection and deterministic error responses instead of mid-stream failures. Implementation highlights: 1) api/handlers/multipart_handler.py implements a two-pass scan: fast header-only pass to enforce per-part size and type heuristics, followed by a streaming handoff that preserves the original stream for allowed parts. 2) Introduced config flags (env) for PART_MAX_BYTES and MULTIPART_TOTAL_MAX_BYTES with sane defaults (10MB per part, 50MB total) and runtime metrics emitted for rejected uploads. 3) Content-type safety: we perform lightweight sniffing (magic bytes + declared header) to avoid accepting text/plain labeled binary blobs; for non-whitelisted types we respond 415 with structured error payload. 4) OpenAI-compat: map legacy form names and accept arrays and singletons to reduce client breakage. 5) Added unit and integration tests covering edge cases and a small e2e run that exercises the streaming generation + tool-call with an uploaded schema file. Checklist: - [x] Implement server-side validation and env flags - [x] Add metrics and structured error responses - [x] Add unit tests and integration e2e - [x] Update docs/compatibility and API reference - [x] Add a hotfix note for incident INT-4421 in changelog

review_comments:
Aaron Lee: Nice consolidation. Can we make PART_MAX_BYTES default to 8MB to match older SDKs?
Priya Kaur: I kept defaults slightly higher (10MB) after spike showed tokenized schema files often exceed 8MB; but made it configurable via env so infra can match historic behavior.
Marta Gomez: Please add a log line at INFO for rejected uploads with the rejection_reason tag; it will help SRE triage.
Priya Kaur: Added metric + structured log in latest commit c5a2f90.
Samir Patel: Security nit: make sure we don't emit file contents in logs.

discussion_resolution:
Addressed reviewer feedback: defaults configurable, metrics/logs added, no file contents logged

release_notes:
Server: multipart uploads now enforce per-part and total payload limits and validate content-type; clients that upload larger files should set PART_MAX_BYTES or switch to external storage and pass URLs. OpenAI-compat field mapping reduces client breakage for legacy integrations.

notes:
This PR was motivated by an incident (INT-4421) where malformed multipart uploads caused worker OOMs. Post-merge, SLO for streaming stability improved in the subsequent canary run. Ops should consider setting stricter PART_MAX_BYTES in high-throughput clusters.

evidence.title: Validate multipart boundaries and enforce file-size/content-type limits on OpenAI-compat tool/file endpoints
evidence.text:
description:
Motivation: several incidents and flaky E2E runs showed that tool/file uploads to the OpenAI-compat endpoints could hang or be accepted with malformed boundaries or incorrect content-type headers, leading to streaming stalls and memory spikes on private deployments. This PR tightens validation for multipart/form-data and chunked transfer uploads, adds enforcement of default file-size limits, and surfaces explicit compatibility-layer error codes so downstream SDKs and clients can handle rejections cleanly. Summary of changes: - Add a multipart boundary presence and consistency check early in request parsing; reject requests missing a boundary with 422 MALFORMED_MULTIPART. - Enforce Content-Type whitelist for tool/file payloads (application/octet-stream, image/*, text/*, application/json, multipart/form-data). Requests with disallowed content-types now return 400 INVALID_CONTENT_TYPE. - Introduce Content-Length and chunked streaming guards. For chunked uploads we now apply per-chunk size ceiling and an aggregate max (default 25MB) and return 413 FILE_TOO_LARGE when exceeded. Limit is configurable via service config and Dedicated/Private can override per-tenant. - Update the OpenAI-compat adapter to normalize incoming form-data to internal file objects, while preserving streaming semantics. Old behavior accepted missing boundary on some clients; new behavior rejects those requests but includes a compatibility hint header (X-Compat-Error) to aid callers. - Add a small in-memory streaming parser for boundary edge-cases to avoid allocating large buffers when boundaries come in split TCP frames. - Bake in tests: unit tests for malformed boundary paths, integration tests with chunked transfer encoding (nginx-style split chunks), e2e test that runs against the compatibility layer. - Documentation: api changelog + compatibility notes and SDK test expectations. Risk & rollout: - Backwards compatible at the protocol level for well-formed clients; some malformed clients will be rejected. To soften rollout we emit the X-Compat-Error hints and a telemetry metric (compat.multipart.reject_count) for 2 weeks before flipping enforcement in some private installs where customers asked for a grace period. - Default file-size cap is conservative (25MB); customers can configure via config.service.file_upload.max_size_bytes. Related: ENG-4132 (multipart resilience), PM-291 (compat ergonomics).

review_comments:
Marco Ruiz: We should document the default max_size_bytes in the config file; otherwise Private customers will be surprised. - ACK, added to config/service_defaults.yaml.
Aisha Thompson: Can we avoid a hard 25MB constant in the runtime? Make sure it's read from the service config with a sensible default. - Done: reads config and falls back to 25MB.
Devon Li: The X-Compat-Error header value should be stable. Use short tokens (e.g., MALFORMED_BOUNDARY) so SDKs can pattern-match. - Updated to use stable tokens in adapters.
Marco Ruiz (follow-up): I hit a flaky test on CI where a boundary split across two frames caused a buffer growth; the streaming parser fix looks good but add a targeted unit test. - Added test and CI passes.
Priya Nair (author): Responded to all review comments and pushed the additional tests and docs updates.

release_notes:
- Enforce multipart boundary and return 422 MALFORMED_MULTIPART for missing/mismatched boundaries.
- Enforce allowed content-types on tool/file endpoints (400 INVALID_CONTENT_TYPE).
- Default file upload size cap of 25MB with 413 FILE_TOO_LARGE error for overage (configurable).
- Compatibility layer emits X-Compat-Error header to help client migration.

evidence.title: add multipart/form-data handling, strict content-type validation, and payload limit enforcement for API tool/file inputs
evidence.text:
description:
Motivation: users integrating tool/function calling and file uploads via the OpenAI-compatibility endpoints were sending a wide variety of content-types and very large multipart requests which caused inconsistent runtime behavior, high memory pressure, and unexpected acceptance of unsupported payloads. This PR introduces a focused, backwards-compatible implementation for multipart/form-data parsing on the OpenAI-compatibility path, strict Content-Type validation for tool/file inputs, and deterministic payload limits both per-file and per-request. Summary of changes: 1) Add a streaming-safe multipart parser that yields parts rather than buffering entire requests; 2) Validate Content-Type of each part (whitelist: text/*, image/*, application/json, application/octet-stream with explicit size checks); 3) Enforce configurable limits: max_file_size (default 10MiB), max_total_request_size (default 50MiB), max_parts_count (default 20). These defaults are conservative and documented; they can be overridden at tenant or route level via API config. 4) Hook validation into the OpenAI-compat layer so existing client integrations get predictable errors (400/413) with structured error bodies when inputs are rejected. 5) Add detailed unit and integration tests and end-to-end tests for streaming uploads and for the dedicated Dedicated/Private ingress paths. Backwards compatibility notes: this does not change the non-multipart JSON body semantics. Existing users who relied on accepting arbitrary large file uploads should update their tenant config or use Redwood Dedicated with higher quotas. Rollout plan: feature-flagged behind feature.enable_multipart_input (off by default); staged rollout to internal dogfood tenants, then gradual roll to 10%, 50%, 100% via config rollout. Checklist: - [x] Streaming-safe multipart parser implemented - [x] Content-Type whitelist + validation errors - [x] Per-file and per-request size enforcement + configurable defaults - [x] OpenAI-compat error mapping and structured error shapes - [x] Tests: unit, integration, e2e - [x] Docs: compatibility notes and config guide - [x] Telemetry: counters for rejected parts and throttled requests - [x] Migration & rollout plan included Testing notes: the multipart parser uses a small constant memory footprint for each active part and yields part metadata to the handler; large parts trigger a streaming drain with early termination (413 response) to avoid OOM. Integration tests exercise combination of binary and text parts, wrong content-types, and boundary cases around the configured limits. Telemetry: added metrics api.multipart.rejected_content_type, api.multipart.rejected_size, api.multipart.accepted_parts and a hist for part sizes. Implementation details: - parser: runtime/multipart/stream_parser.py - validator: api/validation/multipart_validator.py - compat layer: api/openai_compat/input_adapter.py - config: config/defaults/multipart.yaml - docs: docs/openai-compat/multipart.md - tests: tests/unit/test_multipart_parser.py, tests/integration/test_openai_compat_multipart.py Error shape examples (structured output): when a part is rejected we return 413 with a JSON body {"error":{"type":"request_too_large","message":"part exceeds max_file_size","meta":{"part_name":"file","limit_bytes":10485760}}} and 400 for unsupported content-types with type unsupported_media_type. Observability: trace spans added around parse->validate->route dispatch to help pinpoint latency regressions. Related items: Linear ENG-2728 (multipart uploader stability), PM-146 (OpenAI compat feature parity).

review_thread:
Liam Chen: key question — do we need to special-case application/pdf? many partners send PDFs as application/pdf; current whitelist would block it. Suggest adding application/pdf or making whitelist configurable per-tenant.
Aisha Patel: replied — agreed, added application/pdf to tenant_whitelist in config and made default conservative. Added test case + note in docs explaining why binary blobs should be limited.
Ravi Singh: please ensure the validator surfaces clear errors for multipart boundary parsing failures; I saw a flaky crash in an initial run.
Aisha Patel: replied — parser now catches malformed boundary exceptions and returns a 400 with error.type=malformed_multipart and includes low-signal debug id for tracing; updated tests.
Sofia Alvarez: approved — addressed my comments about metrics naming and added a suggestion to include counter tags for tenant_id and route_id.
CI Bot: integration-tests failed on first run due to test harness timeout; rerun completed successfully.
QA: noted an edge case where client SDK retries might double-submit large files; added a recommendation in docs and an optional idempotency header support in adapter.

release_notes:
Added multipart/form-data support on OpenAI-compat API paths with strict content-type validation and configurable per-file and per-request size limits. Default limits: 10MiB per file, 50MiB per request. Feature is behind a feature flag and can be enabled per-tenant. See docs/openai-compat/multipart.md for migration steps.

evidence.title: Enforce MIME sniffing and chunking limits for tool/file uploads (OpenAI-compat layer)
evidence.text:
description:
Motivation: Tool integrations and file attachments coming through the OpenAI-compatibility proxy were accepting overly permissive Content-Type headers and arbitrarily large streaming chunks which caused downstream model handlers to OOM or misclassify payloads. This PR adds deterministic MIME sniffing, per-tool attachment quotas, and streaming chunk size enforcement at the proxy layer so tool authors and user clients get immediate, deterministic rejections instead of opaque runtime errors.

What this changes: - Add a MIME sniffing pass for multipart and single-part uploads that normalizes Content-Type to a safe set and rejects unknown/binary blobs when a tool opts into textual input only. - Implement per-tool max_upload_bytes and max_chunks settings surfaced through the tools registry; defaults applied when not configured. - Enforce max_chunk_bytes for streaming/transfer-encoding style uploads so a single chunk cannot exceed safety limits. - Map legacy OpenAI style headers ("OpenAI-File-Name", "openai-content-type") into our normalized metadata to keep compatibility with existing clients. - Return structured JSON error payloads compatible with OpenAI-compat error shapes (error.code, error.message, error.type) so SDKs can handle programmatic failures. - Add unit and integration tests that exercise multipart boundaries, chunked streams, and header-based compatibility fallbacks.

Checklist: - [x] Add MIME sniffing implementation and canonicalizer in api/proxy/upload_validator.go - [x] Add per-tool config + defaults in services/tools/registry - [x] Add streaming chunk enforcement in streaming/handler.go - [x] Preserve OpenAI compatibility headers and map to internal metadata - [x] Add tests for multipart streaming, single-part file uploads, and header fallbacks - [x] Update docs: redwood-docs/api/file-uploads.md

Compatibility notes: This change preserves behavioral compatibility for existing clients that set Content-Type correctly. Clients relying on implicit server-side assumptions (e.g. sending mixed binary/text under text/plain) will now receive a structured 400 with guidance. Ops: rollout is safe behind a feature flag (features.validate_tool_uploads). Default is off for 48 hours to allow canary release, then on cluster-wide by default.

References: Linear ENG-7382 (upload hardening), incident SUP-4127 (tool-run OOM on binary attachment), and a related follow-up PR will add per-tenant overrides for enterprise Private deployments.

Notes on testing and observations: integration tests found a tokenizer mismatch when content-type was incorrectly marked as "text/plain; charset=utf-16"; MIME canonicalizer now strips charset and uses content sniffed encoding detection for tokenization. CI: one flaky streaming test needed a 200ms backoff retry; I renamed the test to reflect expected semantics.

review_comments:
Marco Liu: Can we add a short-circuit for tools that explicitly accept binary? reasoning: avoid double-copy when proxied to dedicated GPU pool.
Priya (author): Added allow_binary flag per-tool and short-circuit path; added unit tests for the fast path.
Elena Garcia: Please ensure errors follow OpenAI shape and include a "type" that SDKs can switch on. Also confirm 400 vs 415 semantics.
Priya (author): Error payloads now include code/message/type and we return 415 for unsupported media types and 400 for malformed multipart frames.
Samir Patel: lgtm after docs update and a note in the changelog about the 48h feature-flag rollout.

release_notes:
Harden file and tool upload handling: MIME sniffing, per-tool upload quotas, streaming chunk limits, and improved OpenAI-compat error shapes. Feature gated rollout (features.validate_tool_uploads).

evidence.title: streaming-backpressure-and-compat-layer-contenttype-guards-with-tool-payload-throttle
evidence.text:
description:
Motivation: Several recent incidents and internal customer reports highlighted two recurring issues: (1) multipart file uploads used by tool/function-calling flows could cause unbounded memory/queue growth when clients stream faster than worker throughput; (2) the OpenAI-compatibility layer did not consistently enforce content-type and structured-output size constraints which allowed oversized tool payloads to propagate to downstream runners. This PR introduces coordinated protections across the API entrypoint and compatibility shim to make streaming uploads more resilient and to place deterministic limits on tool/file payloads. Summary of changes: - Add streaming backpressure checks at the multipart parser level: per-connection in-flight byte quotas, configurable low/high watermarks, and early 413-style rejections when quotas are exceeded. This prevents request buffering at the gateway and gives predictable failure semantics for fast clients. - Introduce a "X-Tool-Payload-Quota" header that the compat layer will return in streaming responses for tool-calls; the header communicates server-allocated byte budget and remaining allowance so clients can adapt backoff behavior. - Implement server-side throttling for tool file payloads: if a tool upload exceeds its negotiated quota, the server will gracefully terminate the stream and emit structured diagnostics (JSON body with quota_used and limit). - Tighten content-type validation on the OpenAI compatibility endpoint: accept only a small whitelist (multipart/form-data, application/json, application/octet-stream) for attachments and reject ambiguous types (e.g., text/plain with non-UTF8). Also normalize and strip suspicious charset parameters. - Add structured-output size guard for function/tool-calls: the runtime will enforce a serialized size cap for tool responses when wired through the compat layer, with fallback policy support (truncate / error / partial-result). - Add tests (unit + integration) that simulate fast-producer slow-consumer streaming and verify quotas, header propagation, and diagnostic payloads. - Docs and changelog entries for the new headers and configuration knobs. Backwards compatibility: default quotas are conservative and can be raised by config; compat-layer behavior keeps response format stable and only adds the optional header. There is a brief note in CHANGELOG about a new rejected response shape for quota failures so customers can detect and surface them. See release_notes for details. Implementation notes: The backpressure implementation sits in the multipart parser middleware so it applies to both native API routes and the OpenAI-compat gateway. The quota enforcement is per-upload part and per-connection aggregated; we added metrics for quota_rejections, quota_bytes_consumed, and compat_header_emitted. We preferred early reject semantics to avoid head-of-line blocking in the request pipeline. Why this is different from earlier multipart commits: earlier PRs focused on content sniffing and chunking semantics; this PR focuses on operational protection (memory/queue) and explicit client feedback for throttling, plus a small-but-important compat-layer content-type whitelist and structured output cap. 

review_comments:
Evan Turner: Can we avoid adding another global config var? Suggest scoping quota defaults per-route so Hosted customers aren't affected by Private installs.
Priya Desai (author): Scoped the default into route-level config with a global fallback; updated docs and added config examples.
Marta Iqbal: Tests look good. Add an assertion that the quota header is present on partial failures too (helps clients detect retryability).
Priya Desai (author): Added test and a small fix to header emission on error paths.
Rafael Gomez: Small nit: normalizeContentType should treat application/octet-stream; also ensure charset parameters are stripped for comparisons.
Priya Desai (author): Done. Added normalization unit test.

release_notes:
Added server-side streaming quotas for multipart uploads to avoid request buffering; introduced X-Tool-Payload-Quota header to communicate remaining upload budget; compat layer now enforces a strict content-type whitelist for attachments and a serialized structured-output size cap for tool responses. Default quotas are conservative and configurable. Clients should handle 413-like quota rejections by backing off and honoring the header.

notes_for_ops:
Config knobs: multipart.quota.default_bytes, multipart.quota.high_watermark, compat.tool_response.max_serialized_bytes. Metrics: quota_rejections, quota_bytes_consumed, compat_header_emitted. Recommend enabling alert on quota_rejections > 0.1% of multipart requests in first 24h after rollout.

question: What caused an enterprise tenant in Western Europe to suddenly get routed to a Southeast Asia edge during a short mid March 2026 load spike on the vectorization service, adding about 200ms and triggering ingestion timeouts, even though the tenant was supposed to stay in Europe?

evidence.title: Priority-band rehearsal: regional capacity & failover notes
evidence.text:
Context and purpose:
This doc captures the notes from the Priority-Band rehearsal we ran 2026-11-27 -> 11-28. The goal: exercise the regional prioritization rules and fallback bands (what we called 'priority-bands') under a controlled simulated surge so the runbook and oncall handoff are validated. Not a full postmortem — more of a working playbook + action list.

Attendees (live): Aisha P, Marco H, Liang W, Evelyn R, Santiago M, Karthik N (SRE), Jenna L (Solutions Eng).

Agenda:
- 10m: quick status and hypothesis (what we wanted to test)
- 30m: run the simulated client mix against three regions (us-west1, europe-west3, asia-east1)
- 20m: validate automatic fallback to dedicated-capacity pool and the priority-band rule ordering
- 20m: triage unexpected behaviors and collect logs/metrics

What we simulated:
- baseline traffic pattern: 60% hosted-api small-context generations, 30% chat, 10% long-form embedding/rerank bursts.
- injected a 4x surge to europe-west3 over a 12 minute window; concurrently added a spike of long-context requests from a single customer key to simulate heavy-KV-cache usage.
- simulated 15% of nodes preemptible loss in europe-west3 (drain + reboot delay) to test preemption handling.

Observed behavior (summary):
- Priority-band routing correctly moved low-tier traffic to us-west1 and asia-east1 once europe-west3 token latency crossed threshold (250ms p95).
- For long-context requests the automatic fallback to the 'dedicated-long' capacity pool increased tail latency (expected) but preserved throughput; however cost-accounting tags were not consistently attached to rerouted requests (see action item #3).
- Preemption simulation caused 2-minute backlog spike. Autoscaler reclaimed capacity within 4 minutes but did not fully rewarm KV caches causing +30% CPU on surviving instances for the next 6 minutes.
- A small bug in the routing table caused one customer key to be pinned to europe-west3 despite the priority-band rule — root cause appears to be stale map in the policy cache (cache TTL mismatch).

Detailed notes and timestamps:
- 11:03 start: baseline checks all green. Canary traffic probe latency: us-west1 80ms p95, europe-west3 95ms p95, asia-east1 120ms p95.
- 11:10 begin surge injection -> europe-west3 QPS ramp +400% over 3m. By 11:12 europe-west3 p95 token latency 280ms.
- 11:13 routing rules fire: low-tier move to us-west1/asia-east1. Observed 18% increase in us-west1 CPU, 22% in asia-east1. No rate-limit violations.
- 11:15 preemption event (simulated) -> 15% node loss in europe-west3. Autoscaler triggered with target 95% utilization threshold.
- 11:18 backlog spike: request queue depth doubled (from 0.6 -> 1.2 average). Cache-miss rate for KV jumped x4.
- 11:22 fallback to dedicated-long pool: 47 long-context requests routed. Latency p95 for that pool rose from 210ms -> 310ms.
- 11:26 observed policy-cache TTL expired for most keys except one customer; manual cache flush required to free their pinned routing.
- 11:35 ramp-down: europe-west3 QPS back to baseline by 11:40. Metrics show residual elevated CPU until 11:48.

Metrics captured (high-level):
- europe-west3: p95 token latency peak 320ms; avg CPU spike +40%; KV cache miss rate +300% during peak.
- us-west1: traffic increase +22%; p95 token latency stable (+15ms).
- asia-east1: traffic increase +26%; small 3% error-rate bump tied to an old model variant which still existed in model-catalog (see action item #5).

What worked well:
- Priority-band decision engine responded within configured SLOs and routing was smooth for the majority of traffic.
- Autoscaler reacted to node losses and brought capacity back without human intervention.
- Observability: tracing and token-level cost breakdown let us quickly attribute the long-context cost spike to the dedicated-long pool.

Failure modes and glitches:
- Policy cache TTL mismatch (policy-cache TTL config drift between control-plane and edge agents).
- Cost-tagging loss on rerouted requests (some requests lost the tenant billing tag once they traversed fallback pool).
- One old model variant in asia-east1 caused elevated error-rate under load — model-catalog pruning rules not strict enough.
- KV cache rewarm is slow on surviving nodes; we need better prewarming or staged draining to avoid CPU thrash.

Action items (owners and rough ETA):
1) Align policy-cache TTL across control-plane + edge agents; add a cache TTL validation test to CI (owner: Liang Wu, ETA: 2026-12-05).
2) Add a validation step in rollout to ensure model-catalog variant pruning is enforced in all regions (owner: Marco Hernandez, ETA: 2026-12-03).
3) Fix billing tag propagation for fallback pools; ensure request metadata includes cost tags before routing (owner: Evelyn Ross, ETA: 2026-11-30).
4) Experiment with KV prewarm strategies: snapshot-restore vs. gradual traffic drain; run two A/B prewarm tests next week (owner: Karthik N, collaborators: Jenna L, ETA: start 2026-12-01, results by 2026-12-08).
5) Add a synthetic canary that injects long-context requests slowly to dedicated-long pool during ramp-up to avoid immediate tail spikes (owner: Santiago Mora, ETA: 2026-12-02).
6) Update runbook step for manual cache flush to include diagnostic query + automated temporary pin for affected keys (owner: Aisha Patel, ETA: 2026-12-01).

Follow-ups scheduled:
- Short 30m sync Wednesday 2026-12-02 to confirm progress on actions 1,2,3.
- Full rehearsal v2 planned 2026-12-08 where we will: increase simulated preemption to 25%, add a cross-region DDoS-like noisy neighbor, and test the synthetic canary.

Notes to self / loose threads:
- We should consider a new metric: "recovery-latency-to-warm" (time from fallback activation to KV warm state) and attach it to the SLO dashboard.
- Evaluate cost impact of routing long-context to dedicated-long vs. autoscaling existing pool for short windows; need a quick back-of-envelope for finance.
- Check if any customer contracts (enterprise SLAs) require explicit notification when fallback to dedicated occurs (possible legal/CS implications).

Raw links and artifacts collected during the run:
- Traces: link://traces/PRIORITYBAND-2026-11-27 (internal)
- Dashboards: CONFLUENCE-6521#dashboards
- Run logs + recorded terminal session: s3://infra-playbacks/priorityband/2026-11-27/
- Test plan doc: CONFLUENCE-6521/testplan

Quick wins we can ship before next rehearsal:
- Short fix: TTL config sync + add CI check (quick, low-risk)
- Medium: billing tag propagation patch + deploy to canary (medium risk)
- Longer: KV prewarm strategies research and implementation (requires scheduling infra cycles)

End notes: this was a productive run — the majority of the system behaved as intended and our telemetry surfaced the small set of issues quickly. The runbook changes are relatively small but high-value (cache TTL, billing tags, prewarm). Please add anyone I missed to collaborators and ping in #infra-ops if you need early access to logs.

evidence.title: Intermittent streaming slowdowns for Nimbus Payments due to SNAT path bounce between us-east and ap-southeast
evidence.text:
description:
Issue summary:
Customer Nimbus Payments reports intermittent multi-second p95/p99 spikes and occasional request timeouts for streaming completions originating from their us-east tenant when routed to ap-southeast-1 model pools. Impacts mostly streaming responses (chunked / event-stream) where token emission pauses for 2–8s before resuming or times out after 30s.

Impact:
- Several customer production requests saw elevated tail latency affecting payment UI flows.
- Observed increased number of aborted streams and retry traffic from client SDK.
- Customer reported revenue-impacting failures for a small subset of flows.

Environment:
- Customer: Nimbus Payments (dedicated tenant on Redwood Dedicated).
- Affected model pools: ap-southeast-1 serving for redwood-compat-7b and open-llm-chat-13b.
- Traffic path: requests originated from us-east control plane -> egress transit VPC -> ap-southeast-1 serving nodes.

Steps to reproduce (customer-facing):
1) Run high-concurrency streaming completion workload pinned to ap-southeast-1 model pool from a us-east based client.
2) Enable chunked streaming and observe token arrival patterns (p50/p95/p99) via client SDK logs.
3) Notice intermittent multi-second pauses between chunks and occasional SDK-level timeouts.

Observed metrics & logs (excerpt):
- Grafana (obs/streaming) p99 latency spike aligned with egress connection churn (see dashboard link).
- Edge proxy logs: repeated FIN/ACK followed by quick reconnects on same client IP at specific windows.
- Conntrack counters on transit NAT nodes showed port churn and ephemeral port exhaustion warnings around incidents.
- TLS handshake durations spiked by ~300–800ms during events and TCP retransmit counters rose.

Temporary mitigation applied:
- Increased SNAT / ephemeral port allocation on the transit NAT pool for Nimbus tenant (2026-03-12 02:15 UTC).
- Created egress-affinity exception: pinned Nimbus's egress to a smaller subset of stable egress IPs to reduce path-bounce while we investigate.
- Added healthcheck and alert on conntrack utilization for tenant-specific NAT pools.

Next steps / planned fixes:
- Short term: monitor for recurrence and add automated scaling for NAT pools in the transit VPC.
- Medium term: update BGP/eBPF route affinity to avoid asymmetric egress pathing for tenant-bound flows.
- Long term: introduce per-tenant egress autoscaling and refine TCP keepalive/idle timeouts used by edge-proxy to tolerate transient path changes better.

Attachments / links:
- Grafana: https://grafana.redwood/d/streams/nimbus-p99
- Kibana logs: https://kibana.redwood/logs?query=SUP-91234
- Slack thread: #support-nimbus (https://slack.redwood/archives/C12345)

comments:
2026-03-10 09:12 - Aisha Patel (Support): Opened ticket after customer reported multiple streaming stalls. Initial triage suggests cross-region path changes coincide with spikes.
2026-03-11 14:03 - SRE (Liam O'Connor): Observed conntrack warnings on transit NAT; started reproducer to exercise high-concurrency streaming from us-east to ap-southeast.
2026-03-12 02:20 - SRE (Liam O'Connor): Applied temporary SNAT pool increase and egress pinning for Nimbus. Customer reports immediate reduction in observed stalls in canary tests.
2026-03-12 05:47 - Customer (Nimbus Ops): Confirmed reduced failures and fewer timeouts in production, but asked for a durable fix and why this started suddenly.
2026-03-13 11:10 - Network Eng (Priya Sharma): Hypothesis: ephemeral port exhaustion + asymmetric path bounce caused TCP retransmits and TLS handshake latency which delays streaming chunks. Preparing BGP policy change and NAT autoscaling PR.
2026-03-13 15:33 - Support (Aisha Patel): Notified customer of mitigation and next steps; scheduled follow-up for 2026-03-16 to confirm stability after route policy changes.

investigation:
Findings summary: repeated short-lived egress path flips for the tenant were observed at the transit VPC, resulting in new SNAT mappings and TCP connection churn. The combination of per-tenant SNAT pools sized for normal load plus an increase in concurrent streaming connections exhausted ephemeral ports during traffic bursts. When a source port was remapped, downstream servers saw a new 4-tuple and closed prior TLS/TCP connections; clients attempted quick reconnects triggering retransmits and delayed first-token emission. Edge proxy connection reuse semantics amplified the effect, as streaming chunks were tied to a single long-lived TCP connection which, when reset, incurred handshake delays and chunk queuing at the SDK layer.
Root cause hypothesis: insufficient NAT port capacity combined with egress path asymmetry in transit VPC routing rules.
Evidence: conntrack logs, TLS handshake histograms, Grafana graphs aligned to the incident windows, and reduced failure rates after increasing SNAT pool and egress pinning.

resolution:
Temporary mitigation completed 2026-03-12: SNAT pool size increased and egress affinity enforced for Nimbus Payments; immediate reduction in p99 streaming stalls observed. Ongoing work: network team to deploy BGP policy update to stabilize egress pathing and an autoscaler for tenant NAT pools (PR linked). After stabilization period, will roll out improved keepalive/idle tuning on edge-proxy to reduce sensitivity to short path flips.

notes:
Follow-up action: post-mortem draft and runbook changes to add conntrack alerts and per-tenant NAT autoscaling. Customer update scheduled 2026-03-16.

evidence.title: GPU-hour token econ heatmap exploration
evidence.text:
summary:
Exploratory sensitivity matrix and heatmap-style sheet that maps GPU-hour burn and $/1M tokens across instance families and regions for mid-term capacity planning.

content:
Purpose:
This worksheet is an exploratory tool to answer: given a mix of instance families (A100/RTX6000/GPU-eq), region price spreads, and utilization assumptions, what is the implied GPU-hour burn and $/1M tokens across scenarios? The goal is to identify breakpoints where routing policy should prefer cheaper regions or different instance families, and where Dedicated commitments make sense.

Assumptions (baseline):
- Model mix: 60% generation (variable seq length), 30% chat (latency-sensitive), 10% embeddings/batching.
- Token distribution: median request = 120 tokens input, 300 tokens output for generation; chat = 40 in / 80 out.
- Effective throughput per GPU-hour (baseline perf profile):
  - a100-80GB: 45k tokens/sec sustained aggregate (mixed workloads), 162M tokens/hour
  - rtx-6000-48GB: 22k tokens/sec, 79.2M tokens/hour
  - gpu-eq-light (quantized): 15k tokens/sec, 54M tokens/hour
- Cloud list $/GPU-hour (example):
  - us-east-1 a100-80: $24.00/hr (on-demand), $12.00/hr (reserved blended)
  - europe-west-1 a100-80: $28.00/hr, $14.00/hr reserved
  - us-west-2 rtx-6000: $8.50/hr, $5.50/hr reserved
  - asia-southeast-1 gpu-eq-light: $6.00/hr, $4.00/hr reserved
- Utilization target buckets: low=30%, mid=60%, high=85% (applies to committed pool).
- Overhead & non-token work multiplier: +8% GPU-hour for control plane and I/O overhead.

Key calculated metrics (explicit formulas shown as plain text):
- tokens_per_gpu_hour = tokens_per_sec * 3600 * utilization
- effective_gpu_hour_cost = $/GPU-hour * (1 + overhead)
- $/1M_tokens = effective_gpu_hour_cost / (tokens_per_gpu_hour / 1_000_000)
- implied_token_passthrough = peak-concurrency headroom adjustments (applied as utilization shrinkage under tail-latency SLOs)

Sample scenario table (baseline utilization = 60%):
| region | instance | $/GPUh | tokens/h (raw) | tokens/h (utilized) | effective $/GPUh | $/1M tokens | notes |
us-east-1 | a100-80 | 24.00 | 162,000,000 | 97,200,000 | 25.92 | 0.2668 | baseline high perf
eu-west-1 | a100-80 | 28.00 | 162,000,000 | 97,200,000 | 30.24 | 0.3111 | europe premium
us-west-2 | rtx-6000 | 8.50  | 79,200,000  | 47,520,000  | 9.18  | 0.1932 | lower per-hour cost but half throughput
asia-southeast-1 | gpu-eq-light | 6.00 | 54,000,000 | 32,400,000 | 6.48 | 0.2000 | quantized variant

Observations from example numbers:
- Even though rtx-6000 and gpu-eq-light have lower $/GPUh, their lower token throughput per hour can produce similar or worse $/1M tokens compared to a100 in regions with modest price spreads.
- Europe premium on a100 pushes $/1M above 30c; routing latency-sensitive chat to eu-west1 should be weighed against the incremental cost.
- Quantized variants narrow cost but may introduce quality/regression risk; treat as compatible only for batch/embedding workloads initially.

Sensitivity matrix approach:
- Dimensions: Region price delta (±30%), Utilization (30/60/85%), Model efficiency variance (±20% tokens/sec).
- For each cell compute percent delta in $/1M tokens relative to baseline. Generate heatmap coloring: green < -10% (cheaper), amber between -10% and +10%, red > +10% (expensive).

Example sensitivity bullets (high level):
- Under low utilization (30%), $/1M for a100 in us-east-1 increases ~+40% compared to baseline because tokens_per_gpu_hour halves. Cheaper instance types become more attractive for spiky bursty workloads.
- Under +20% model efficiency (faster kernels / quantization gains), rtx-6000 moves from 0.193 $/1M to ~0.161 $/1M, making mid-tier instances compelling at scale.
- Regional spot windows: if spot can reduce $/GPUh by >50% for >=20% of our capacity, effective blended $/1M drops materially; but reliability constraints increase tail latency risk.

Operational scenarios to evaluate (each row corresponds to a simulation tab in the sheet):
- Conservative reserved-heavy: 70% reserved in primary region, 30% on-demand cross-region failover. Model allocation pins high-throughput models to reserved pool.
- Cost-optimal opportunistic: route non-latency batch to cheapest region/instance given a quality threshold. Use conservative headroom for canary.
- Latency-first hybrid: chat routed to low-latency a100 pockets (lower utilization but higher $/1M), batch/embeddings to quantized pools.

Decision heuristics derived from heatmap:
- If $/1M in fallback region <= baseline + 5% and network RTT delta <= 60ms, prefer fallback for non-chat workloads.
- If utilization for any committed pool falls below 45% for 30 days, downscale reserved profile or reassign workloads (use A/B routing to shift batch).
- Set a threshold: if rtx-6000 $/1M <= a100 $/1M * 0.9, pilot model variant on rtx-6000 for 2 weeks and evaluate quality/regression metrics.

Open questions / caveats:
- Token/sec numbers are system-averages; per-model profiles vary widely. Need per-model perf profiles for accurate mapping (hook to model catalog).
- Network egress and cross-region data transfer costs not modeled here; add delta columns when considering cross-region routing.
- Headroom for cold-starts and auto-scaling transient capacity assumed inside utilization; real tails can require provisioned spare capacity.

Next steps / action items:
- Engineering: generate per-model tokens/sec and latency profile export (ticket JIRA-ML-224).
- Finance: provide committed pricing tiers for upcoming contract negotiations for eu-west-1 and asia-southeast-1.
- Product: define workload classification labels for routing (chat/low-latency vs batch/throughput vs embeddings).
- Ops: build a small simulation harness to iterate on the sensitivity matrix and export heatmap CSV for dashboarding.

Appendix: quick-check formulas to copy into sheet cells (Excel/Sheets friendly):
- tokens_per_gpu_hour = tokens_per_sec * 3600 * utilization
- effective_cost = gpu_hour_price * (1 + overhead_fraction)
- cost_per_1M = effective_cost / (tokens_per_gpu_hour / 1000000)

Raw sample numbers for quick paste (CSV style):
region,instance,gpu_hour_price,tokens_per_sec,utilization,overhead_fraction
us-east-1,a100-80,24,45000,0.60,0.08
eu-west-1,a100-80,28,45000,0.60,0.08
us-west-2,rtx-6000,8.5,22000,0.60,0.08
asia-southeast-1,gpu-eq-light,6,15000,0.60,0.08

Notes for reviewers: this is intentionally exploratory and uses rounded example numbers. Replace cloud price inputs with the latest billing/export and model perf with infra-perf team outputs before making capacity commitments.

Document history: created by Ethan Kim 2025-09-18; iterated with Aisha and Marco during infra planning week; current draft 2026-02-15 includes sensitivity matrix outline for review.

evidence.title: Surge shepherding simulation and regional handoff notes
evidence.text:
Purpose:
Quick recap and decisions from the cross-regional surge shepherding simulation run on 2026-06-24. This doc is a working log: outcomes, surprises, and a concrete handoff checklist for oncall and capacity ops to adopt into the weekday shift.

Attendees (short):
- Marisol (owner)
- Ethan (fleet ops)
- Priya (routing + orchestration)
- Samir (cost + capacity forecasting)
- Jules (SRE / observability)
- Observers: two solutions eng interns

High-level goal:
- Validate the "shepherding" flow for short-lived high-traffic tenant bursts: detect surge, pre-warm regional pools, migrate lower-priority workloads, and ensure degraded but acceptable latency for PLG traffic while preserving SLAs for enterprise tenants.

Simulation setup:
- Timebox: 90 minutes (14:00–15:30 PDT)
- Regions involved: us-west1 (primary), europe-west3 (spillover), us-east4 (reserve)
- Models used: rdx-7b-int8 (latency-sensitive), rdx-13b-q4 (costy), rdx-3b (background preemptible)
- Load profile: synthetic tenant X ramp (0 -> 600 RPS over 6 min), tail requests with prompt length 1024 tokens, 20% streaming responses
- Injected faults: 1 simulated node OOM in us-west1 at T+12m, 2x transient network jitter in europe-west3 at T+27m

Observations / timeline highlights:
1) Detection & signal fidelity (0–2m):
- Surge detection triggered at +90s using combined token-level increase + per-tenant concurrency spike. Good: low false positive. Minor: single noisy metric from prefix cache miss caused transient early trigger at +45s (false alarm) — caused a short-lived prewarm but no harm.

2) Warmup behavior (2–8m):
- Pre-warm policy correctly allocated 8 cold GPUs in us-west1. Warmup time averaged 45s per device for rdx-7b-int8.
- Observation: cold start variance correlated with local image pull throttling on a subset of nodes. Suggest pinning warmup images to local disk for high-sensitivity tenants.

3) Routing and spillover (8–20m):
- When us-west1 reached 85% util, smart-router moved 22% of new requests to europe-west3. Europe saw 1.7x latency increase (P50 120ms -> 210ms), P99 degradation within SLO but close to threshold for streaming paths.
- Failover to us-east4 reserve performed as designed but there was a 30s period where token accounting lags caused minor double-counting in cost metrics (billing pipeline ticketed).

4) Fault injection effects (12m and 27m):
- The simulated OOM forced immediate evictions of background preemptible workloads; shepherding rules successfully bumped lower-priority work. No enterprise tenant impact observed.
- Network jitter in europe-west3 amplified tail latencies; the system did not automatically shift more traffic back to us-west1 until manual override at +35m. Root cause: existing circuit-breaker cooldown was too conservative.

Metrics: (selected snapshots)
- Peak GPU utilization (us-west1): 96% (sustained 4m)
- Average warmup time per device: 45s (stddev 12s)
- P50 request latency (ramp): 78ms -> 140ms after spillover
- P99 tail latency (streaming): 1.2s -> 1.9s under jitter
- Cost delta (simulated) for the surge window: +21% infra cost vs baseline (driven by warmup + cross-region egress)

What surprised us:
- Image pull throttling on a small fraction of nodes (ISP-level variance) caused heterogeneous warmup times — we assumed cold images would be uniformly fast.
- Billing double-counting window due to token-accounting lag when route changes happen quickly — manifests as transient spikes in customer cost dashboards.
- Circuit-breaker cooldown blocked automated reroute for 30s even though downstream metrics suggested immediate action.

Decisions and immediate changes (agreed in meeting):
1) Warmup image strategy: add a lightweight prefetch artifact that is <12MB and prioritized on refresh; implement as a fallback in warmup path. Owner: Ethan. Due: 2026-06-28. JIRA: INFRA-4890.
2) Reduce circuit-breaker cooldown for region routing from 30s -> 10s for streaming-heavy routes. Owner: Priya. Due: 2026-06-26.
3) Billing token-accounting: add a guard that tags requests during route transitions to avoid double-counting; gate in billing pipeline and add a 10s reconciliation window. Owner: Samir. Due: 2026-07-02.
4) Observability: add a warmup variance dashboard, surface image-pull latency per host. Jules to prototype dashboard tiles and alert thresholds. Due: 2026-07-01.

Handoff checklist for oncall and capacity ops (new items to be added to weekday shiftbook):
- When surge alert fires, confirm warmup pool size and check image-pull latency tile. If variance > 20s, escalate to Ethan and open "warmup-variance" Slack thread in #fleet-ops.
- If routing spillover occurs and europe P99 > 1.5s, consider manual preference to us-east4 reserve and notify Priya.
- For billing anomalies (one-off spikes during route changes) open ticket INFRA-BILL-2026 and notify finance dashboard owner.

Action items (owner / due / quick notes):
- Ethan: implement 12MB prefetch fallback in warmup path (INFRA-4890) / 2026-06-28 / quick patch + canary on staging.
- Priya: update circuit-breaker cooldowns + add unit test for immediate reroute heuristic / 2026-06-26.
- Samir: add 10s reconciliation tag and update billing downstream docs / 2026-07-02.
- Jules: dashboard tiles for warmup variance and image-pull latency; playbook alert thresholds / 2026-07-01.
- Marisol: update weekday shiftbook with handoff checklist and run a 30-min training with capacity ops / 2026-07-05.

Open questions for follow-up:
- Do we want an explicit "emergency warmup pool" (hot-warm buffer) for PLG tenants or rely on pre-warm + rapid image pull? Tradeoffs: cost vs faster ramp. Samir to produce cost sensitivity next week.
- Can edge-cache of container artifacts be standardized across clouds to reduce image-pull spikes? Need infra procurement + cloud vendor input.

Notes to self / informal:
- Consider a short-term scriplet to detect image-pull slowness and kick a local docker pull from a different mirror — low-risk and quick.
- Try the reroute heuristic in integration cluster first; add a canary percent before global rollout.

Appendix (links):
- Full simulation logs (S3): s3://redwood-infra/simulations/surge-2026-06-24/logs
- Grafana dashboard snapshot: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/SurgeSim/2026-06-24
- PR with warmup prefetch prototype: https://github.com/redwood-inference/ops/pull/513

Status: drafting into playbook. Once owners complete their items, convert to final playbook page and link from runbook hub.

Quick wins we can ship this week: warmup prefetch, circuit-breaker cooldown change, a short billing reconciliation guard. Prioritize 1) prefetch + 2) cooldown.

If anything urgent after hours: ping #fleet-ops and tag @Ethan and @Marisol.

evidence.title: incidents
evidence.text:
incident-bot: ALERT — Increased KMS latency and 503s observed for GCP KMS in europe-west1. Affected: service startups (signing), live request signing. Error spike starting 2026-03-15T10:02:00Z. Paging oncall.
ops-bot: Paging @priya.k (SRE oncall) :rotating_light: — check startup/signing failures in logs.
priya.k: I’m on it. Looking at ingress and instance startup errors now. Early look: a lot of `KMS_UNAVAILABLE` and `deadline exceeded` from kms.googleapis.com.
jamal: Confirming — seeing startup tasks stuck waiting for keyring access, retries saturating worker threads.
priya.k: Impact: new pods in europe-west1 failing init (sidecar signing) causing 503/502 for customers on initial requests. Some long-lived services are ok because they already had cached keys.
maeve: Is this limited to europe-west1?
priya.k: So far yes — europe-west1 primarily. I see elevated latencies for kms.googleapis.com in our monitoring, high error rate visible in cloudtrace.
dave.m: Queuing note: client SDK does 3 quick retries then marks instance unhealthy. That fast retry loop is amplifying failures.
jamal: Immediate mitigation idea: increase client retry backoff and allow startup to continue without blocking on KMS for a short window (defer signing until ready).
priya.k: Agreed. Two-step plan: 1) Hotfix config to make sidecar tolerate KMS timeouts at startup (fallback to delayed signing). 2) Add aggressive exponential backoff and jitter to SDK (avoid thundering herd).
maeve: Do we have a way to warm keys locally so mid-flight requests succeed?
dave.m: We have cached ephemeral keys in Vault for some fleets — can enable cache-first mode for these clusters while KMS recovers. Requires config push.
ops-bot: Running runbook step: enable kcache fallback = true for cluster europe-west1 (command below).
```
# enable ephemeral key cache fallback
kubectl -n infra set env daemonset/signing-sidecar KCACHE_FALLBACK=true --context=gke-europe-west1
```
priya.k: Applying that now to signing-sidecar daemonset (rolling update set to maxUnavailable=1). Pushing patch to make startup non-blocking in parallel.
jamal: Noted. Also opening ticket with GCP support — escalating KMS/Cloud KMS latencies. Tagging cloud-support.
cloud-support: Received. GCP: Case #CS-2026-3579 — investigating regional control plane degradation affecting KMS; will update within 30m.
maeve: Customer impact summary for now: intermittent 502/503 on initial requests for some tenants in eu region over last 12 minutes. No data loss reported. Adding to incident status page.
priya.k: Live mitigation checklist executed: - enabled KCACHE_FALLBACK - increased SDK retry backoff to base 500ms, max 8s - 0-downtime restart of signing-sidecar with non-blocking init - routed new traffic to eu-west2 for critical customers (migration toggle).
dave.m: Code snippet we rolled (hotfix):
```
// tolerate KMS timeouts during startup
if (!kms.ready() && env.KCACHE_FALLBACK == "true") {
  log.info("KMS unavailable; enabling local cache fallback for startup")
  signingService.enableLocalCache()
} else {
  signingService.blockUntilKeyAvailable(timeout=30000)
}
```
priya.k: After config change we see new pods coming up successfully. Error rate for signing down from 45% -> 8% over 12 minutes.
jamal: Still seeing some spikes in requests that require immediate KMS access — for those we've toggled traffic to eu-west2 as fallback.
maeve: Any concern about cache serving stale keys / security? What TTL are we using?
dave.m: Cache TTL is 5m by default. For emergency mode we keep it strict (5m) and force revalidation once KMS healthy. Documented in runbook.
priya.k: Notifying account teams and posting on status page draft: "We are investigating increased KMS latencies in GCP europe-west1 that caused intermittent startup and signing errors for some services. Mitigations applied; partial recovery observed. Working with GCP on root cause."
ops-bot: statuspage update published to internal incident channel and external status page (under maintenance).
cloud-support: GCP update: "We are seeing elevated control plane latency due to regional networking issue impacting KMS frontends. Engineers are rolling mitigations; no ETA yet for full restoration."
jamal: Next steps: 1) Keep KCACHE_FALLBACK enabled until GCP confirms healthy 2) Patch client SDK to exponential backoff and bump retry ceiling 3) Postmortem: consider adding multi-region KMS routing and local key cache warm at boot 4) Add detection alert for KMS startup failures specifically.
maeve: I'm taking the handoff for the next 4 hours. @priya.k please collect logs and timeline for the postmortem. @dave.m please coordinate the SDK patch PR and fast rollback plan.
priya.k: On it. Capturing timeline: incident start 2026-03-15T10:02Z; KCACHE_FALLBACK enabled 2026-03-15T10:08Z; traffic routed to eu-west2 for some tenants 10:12Z; error rate reduced by 10:20Z.
dave.m: Will open PR with retry/backoff improvements and integration test for startup path by EOD.
maeve: Notifying legal/product about customers impacted and preparing communication for those with committed SLAs. No major revenue incidents yet, just increased error rates.
priya.k: Logging follow-up actions into the incident tracker: - postmortem owner: priya.k - SDK patch owner: dave.m - infra change to multi-region KMS failover: jamal
ops-bot: Incident: set status = "mitigated" (partial) — monitoring for full recovery.
incident-bot: INCIDENT RESOLVED (partial mitigation) — KMS errors reduced; continue monitoring.
maeve: I'll stay on watch and update when GCP gives final resolution. Handoff complete to @maeve. :white_check_mark:
priya.k: Thanks team — good coordination. Will assemble postmortem and include recommendations: stricter startup timeouts, cache-first bootstrap, and multi-region signing strategy.

question: In our hosted chat streaming, a corporate gateway forces the stream into a polling style connection and after a reconnect the assistant reply consistently loses the last couple sentences and the final completion status never arrives; what is the recommended short term mitigation for customers until a server side fix is deployed?

evidence.title: SSE session-handoff causes trailing silence + JSON fragment split when reconnecting behind enterprise proxy
evidence.text:
description:
Issue summary: Customer reports that when a browser client behind an enterprise reverse proxy (corporate NGN/inspect proxy) reconnects an SSE stream, the final JSON choice is sometimes split across two fragments and the stream ends with 4-6s of trailing silence before an EOF event. Impact: downstream application shows 'incomplete assistant response' and discards last sentence in 12% of reconnect events.

Impact: BrightChat AI's customer-facing chat widget is intermittently missing the last sentence after network blips, causing UX regressions for end-users. Several paid enterprise customers noticed degraded conversational quality.

Environment: prod traffic routed through customer's corporate proxy chain -> customer edge -> Redwood API Gateway -> serving runtime. Client SDK: web-sdk@1.8.2 (EventSource-based SSE).

Observed behavior: on reconnect, server emits resume event and then a sequence of data chunks. A JSON metadata chunk that includes 'finish_reason' sometimes arrives split (e.g., '{"choices":[{"text":"...","finish_reason":"' then 'length"}]}'), causing client JSON parse errors or partial choice rendering. Additionally, there is a multi-second gap (4-6s) of no data before final EOF event in a subset of sessions.

Expected behavior: resume and finalization messages should be emitted as complete JSON tokens and the stream should deliver EOF promptly (sub-second) after final content.

Steps to reproduce: 1) Use web-sdk@1.8.2 behind an enterprise transparent proxy that performs TLS inspection and connection pooling. 2) Initiate long streaming generation (approx 400-800 tokens) with SSE. 3) Simulate short network blip (TCP FIN then reconnect, or client re-establish EventSource). 4) Observe client-side partial JSON parse or silent gap before EOF.

Notes: Customer provided an HAR, tcpdump slices from their edge, and a minimal reproduction app. The problem is not consistently reproducible in staging where proxy chain is absent.

steps_to_reproduce:
Open BrightChat web widget (web-sdk@1.8.2) behind corporate proxy
Send a long prompt to trigger streaming (>400 tokens)
Force a short network disconnect (toggle client network or simulate FIN)
Allow client to reconnect automatically and observe final JSON and EOF timing

observed_behavior:
Final JSON metadata chunk sometimes arrives split across multiple SSE data frames; client JSON.parse fails or truncates last sentence. In ~12% of reconnects, there is a 4-6s gap of no bytes before server sends EOF event.

expected_behavior:
Resume and terminal events arrive intact in the same data frame(s) or in-order without mid-fragment splits. EOF emitted within 500ms of final token under normal path.

logs:
client-har: request id 9a3b-20260309.har (attached) - shows two 'data:' lines splitting terminal JSON
tcpdump-slice: edge-9a3b-20260309.pcap (attached) - shows proxy reusing keepalive connection and 2nd fragment delayed
gateway-log: gw-req-2026-03-09-9a3b - upstream resumed, served resume_token=xyz, final_sent=true

investigation_notes:
03/10 09:15 - Support (Asha): validated customer HAR; reproduced client parse error locally when inserting 1-2 byte MTU splits in SSE frames.
03/10 13:40 - SRE (Liam): observed that our HTTP/1.1 SSE framing uses chunked encoding; some corporate proxies coalesce and re-chunk payloads causing split JSON sequences across TCP writes.
03/10 15:05 - Eng (Marta): hypothesis: proxy connection pooling + buffering leads to artificial pause before final chunk is flushed. Also saw keepalive COALESCE behavior on proxy (github.com/proxy-vendor/issue/432).
03/11 10:30 - Experiment: Add explicit '\n\n' delimiter between SSE 'data:' blocks for metadata; in controlled repro this reduced JSON parse failures but the pause still appeared in 3% of cases.
03/11 14:00 - Confirmed correlation between TLS inspection appliance (vendor: NetInspect) and higher reproduction rate. Vendor docs mention stream coalescing for performance.
Linked Slack thread: #support (thread SUP-128999) and #infra (messages: p01)

comments:
2026-03-10 09:22 - Asha Kumar (Support): Customer attached HAR and pcap. They say ~1 in 8 reconnects fail with last sentence missing. Requested SDK and server logs.
2026-03-10 12:05 - Liam O'Connor (SRE): I pulled gateway logs for the request ids in the HAR. Server emitted final JSON in one write, but the TCP trace shows proxy split the payload into two segments and delayed the second by ~4.2s.
2026-03-10 15:20 - Marta Alvarez (Engineers): I've pushed an experiment branch to the serving runtime to force a flush after terminal chunk. Requesting QA to validate with customer's repro harness.
2026-03-11 11:00 - BrightChat (Customer): We validated the SDK patch - parse errors reduced but still intermittently a trailing gap. We can coordinate to whitelist traffic from TLS inspection appliance for a test window.
2026-03-11 16:30 - Liam O'Connor (SRE): Deployed hotfix to prod (serving-runtime PR 900) that explicitly emits an extra zero-length SSE data frame and forces connection flush at end-of-stream. Monitoring for 48h.
2026-03-12 09:05 - Asha Kumar (Support): Customer confirmed fix: no missing final sentence observed in 96h of traffic during test window after hotfix and vendor appliance whitelist. Marking resolved and adding runbook item.

resolution:
Hotfix deployed: serving-runtime forces flush and emits zero-length SSE marker at stream end. JS SDK updated with delimiter guard to reduce parse risk. Follow-up: add runbook entry and telemetry to detect re-chunked terminal events. Customer validated fix under test window; recommended mitigation for other enterprise customers is to whitelist Redwood streams or disable coalescing on proxy.

follow_up_actions:
Create infra alert to detect final-chunk >1s delays (INFRA-STREAM-ALRT)
Add runbook steps for Support for proxy-related streaming issues
Rollout SDK delimiter change in next minor release (target 2026-04-01)
Reach out to proxy vendors with reproduction data and recommended config

evidence.title: Long-poll fallback closes early, truncating streamed tail on reconnect
evidence.text:
description:
Issue summary: Customer reports that when their corporate edge rewrites Streaming SSE to a long-poll fallback path, the last ~1-2 sentences of responses are consistently missing after a reconnect.

Impact: Intermittent data loss for streaming responses behind certain proxies; affects customer-facing assistant content (missing trailing sentences). Reported by a Dedicated customer (NimbusDocs) using the hosted API through a corporate proxy that downgrades SSE to HTTP long-polling.

Observed behavior: Client receives streamed tokens, then connection is torn down by edge for long-poll fallback. When the session resumes the service returns an early 204/OK and the final trailer event (closing marker/end metadata) is not delivered to the client. Result: truncated final paragraph and absent terminal metadata (choice.finish_reason).

Expected behavior: Fallback path should replay or proxy through the complete trailing chunks or the server should re-emit terminal events after reconstitution so the client receives the full final sentence and closing metadata.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Customer environment: desktop app behind corporate proxy that strips SSE and does long-polling; use proxy that rewrites HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/1.0 and closes keepalive after 15s.
2) Open a streaming chat session against the Redwood hosted API with Accept: text/event-stream and keepalive enabled; send a prompt that yields a 60-120 token final paragraph.
3) Trigger a controlled network interruption to force the proxy to close and re-establish the HTTP connection (simulate edge path change or probe).
4) Observe on the client: streaming resumes but final 1-2 sentences are missing; server logs show a short-lived long-poll request that returns without the closing trailer event.
5) Reproduce reliably by toggling the proxy keepalive interval in synthetic lab; behavior observed ~7/10 runs.

logs:
[2026-03-10T14:08:12Z] proxy edge: Upstream accepted, id=xyz-7
[2026-03-10T14:08:26Z] client -> proxy: Connection close by proxy (keepalive expiry) (15s)
[2026-03-10T14:08:26Z] proxy -> rt-proxy: new long-poll /v1/stream?session=abc returning 200 OK (early-close)
[2026-03-10T14:08:26Z] rt-proxy: stream-session abc resumed; last-kv-checkpoint=0x7f1; trailer_flag=false
[2026-03-10T14:08:27Z] serving-runtime: produced final-choice tokens, emitted trailer meta (choice.finish_reason=length)
[2026-03-10T14:08:27Z] rt-proxy: upstream write failed: client closed connection; skipping trailer emission on long-poll path

investigation_notes:
Hypothesis 1: Long-poll fallback path short-circuits trailer emission when client socket indicates close; race between runtime's trailer write and proxy long-poll response commit.
Hypothesis 2: Proxy/edge performs an extra connection-level close that causes rt-proxy to treat resumed session as ephemeral and drop final metadata to avoid blocking write (backpressure handling path).
Repro steps validated in internal staging with our test proxy (haproxy) reproducing 80% of runs when keepalive <= 20s.
Observed difference vs normal SSE: SSE code path uses chunked transfer with streaming flush; long-poll path uses buffered response commit and currently lacks explicit trailer re-synthesis when the client reconnection occurs.
Logs indicate serving-runtime did emit finish trailer but rt-proxy logged upstream write failure before it could sink to the client long-poll response body.
