evidence.title: Condensed Narrative Mode + Hybrid Rendering for High-Density Time-series
evidence.text:
summary:
Add a new 'Condensed Narrative' accessibility mode for time-series charts that generates lightweight human-readable summaries for screen readers, paired with a hybrid rendering strategy (canvas decimation + SVG focus overlays) to improve interactive perf on very large series.

description:
Problem:
- High-density time-series (50k+ points) create heavy DOM and long paint times. Screen reader users get no concise context (raw axis values and long tables are noisy).
- We need a pattern in the design system that: 1) provides accessible, human-focused summaries of trends/anomalies; 2) reduces DOM/ARIA verbosity; 3) keeps interactive pan/zoom and tooltip fidelity for sighted users; 4) degrades gracefully on low-power devices.

Proposal:
- Condensed Narrative Mode (CNM): an optional chart mode that exposes a single accessible summary block per chart containing a short natural-language description (3-5 sentences) describing the dominant trend, latest value delta, detected anomalies (count + timestamps), and recommended follow-ups. The block is the primary screen-reader target (aria-live polite) instead of exposing every data point.
- Narrative templates: small, testable templates that cover monotonic trends, seasonal patterns, spikes/plateaus, and flatness. Maintain a templating spec in docs for consistency across charts.
- Hybrid Rendering Strategy: default visible layer uses decimated canvas drawing for the full series (fast paint, minimal DOM). An overlay SVG layer renders focus elements (selection handles, legend markers, hover lines) for crisp interaction and accessibility hooks (ARIA roles on handles, not on thousands of points).
- Keyboard / Focus model: keyboard focus lands on chart container -> control menu -> condensed narrative -> press Enter to toggle focus to interactive overlay (small number of interactive elements only).
- Energy and low-power mode: auto-enable more aggressive decimation on devices reporting reduced power mode or when battery low to preserve responsiveness.

Acceptance criteria:
- Accessibility:
  - Screen reader reads condensed narrative within 300ms of chart render with aria-live polite.
  - Narrative covers: overall direction (rise/fall/flat), percent change over visible window, up to 3 anomalies with timestamps, and a short CTA if applicable.
  - Keyboard traversal: chart container -> narrative -> overlay elements. Verified in VoiceOver (Mac), NVDA (Windows), TalkBack (Android web).
- Performance:
  - For a 100k-point series, initial render <= 150ms on a mid-range laptop (cold load) and pan/zoom frame updates <= 80ms for typical viewport changes.
  - DOM node reduction: at least 90% fewer interactive DOM nodes vs naive per-point SVG rendering for large series.
- Visual parity:
  - Hover/tooltip content for focused points must match existing tooltip copy and accept the same structured output schema.
- Rollout / Feature flagging:
  - Implementation behind flag `chart.condensedNarrative` and `chart.hybridRendering` for staged rollout.

Design deliverables:
- Figma spec with narrative templates + examples for 5 series archetypes (monotonic rise, cyclical, noisy with spikes, plateau then drop, sparse with outliers). Link: https://www.figma.com/file/EXAMPLE/condensed-narrative-charts (mock).
- Component API surface (design): Chart props: {mode: 'default'|'condensedNarrative', narrativeTemplates: string[], decimationStrategy: 'largest-triangle'|'reservoir', lowPowerThreshold: number}. (Will be turned into a small prop spec doc for engineers.)

Engineering notes / constraints:
- Backend: algorithm to produce narrative must run client-side using precomputed summary stats (min/max/mean/median/percentile/spike-count) passed down by telemetry or computed from visible window. Avoid O(n) work on main thread for huge series—use WebWorker for full recompute or incremental summaries from server.
- Graphics: use an offscreen canvas where available and CompositeLayers pattern to composite canvas + SVG overlays.
- Metrics: emit telemetry events when CNM is used, and capture perceived latency via RUM.

QA checklist:
- Manual a11y test on VoiceOver, NVDA, TalkBack for each archetype.
- Automated axe-core smoke tests for the chart container and narrative block.
- Performance bench: synthetic harness to replay 100k points and measure TTFP and p95 interaction latency.

Dependencies:
- ENG-71240 (rendering kernel upgrades for offscreen canvas)
- ENG-70512 (telemetry: series summaries endpoint)

Risks & mitigations:
- Risk: Narrative template may oversimplify and hide edge cases. Mitigation: provide a verbatim 'data inspector' button that opens raw values for power users and persists in UI for analysts.
- Risk: Over-aggressive decimation loses important spikes. Mitigation: anomaly-preserving decimation (keep top-k largest residuals) and surfacing flagged timestamps in narrative.

Rollout plan:
- Phase 1: Internal dogfood behind flags for design/eng (10% of org).
- Phase 2: Beta group (customers who opt in) with telemetry tracking for 2 weeks.
- Phase 3: Gradual rollout to 50% then 100% if error and regressions are acceptable.

Links and artifacts:
- Figma: https://www.figma.com/file/EXAMPLE/condensed-narrative-charts
- Spec doc (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/CHART/Condensed+Narrative+Mode
- Prototype PR (engineering): https://github.com/redwood-inference/charts/pull/987
- Accessibility checklist: https://docs.redwood.ai/a11y/charting-guidelines


comments:
2026-02-12 - Luca Moreno: Initial feasibility OK. Need ENG to validate offscreen canvas support across our supported browsers.
2026-02-25 - Mx. Rivera (Accessibility): Recommend adding an explicit 'narrative verbosity' setting (short|medium|detailed) for users requiring more context.
2026-03-02 - Product: Tie CTA suggestions in narratives to existing alerting templates so product teams can hook in runbooks.
2026-03-10 - Design review: Update Figma with examples of low-power rendering and keyboard flow; ensure visual focus indicator on overlay controls is 3:1 contrast at minimum.

evidence.title: eng-platform
evidence.text:
Allison Grant: Dropping early cache dashboards here for eyes 👀 https://grafana.redwood-internal/p/dash-cache-telemetry-v0 (behind VPN). Looking for feedback on panels + filters before we bake alerts. Current top-level filters: `deployment_mode`, `model`, `route_id` (allowlisted), `region` (limited set). Anything missing / any panels confusing?

Sergio Costa: skimmed. Overall solid. A few notes:
- I really want a model-family breakdown (e.g. llama / mistral / qwen) in addition to specific model_version. Otherwise comparisons are noisy when versions churn.
- region breakdown needs to be front + center, not buried. Most cache regressions we’ve seen are locality/placement.
- prompt length buckets: can we get a consistent `prompt_len_bucket` tag on the hist + the hit-rate panel? Right now I only see it on the reuse depth histogram.

Logan Wright: +1 on prompt length bucket. The “overall hit-rate” graph is hard to interpret without the request shape mix.
Also: route_id filter is useful but we have to be careful w/ cardinality. Are we already aggregating to route_group for hosted?

Nadia Rahman: re: model family — we can add a derived label in dashboards (regex on `model_id`) but would prefer runtime/gateway to emit an explicit `model_family` from the allowlist so we don’t end up with 15 different regex variants across dashboards.
On prompt buckets: standards doc proposes: `prompt_len_bucket` = {"0-256","257-512","513-1k","1k-2k","2k-4k","4k-8k","8k+"} and we should reuse across all cache metrics.

Ethan Park: region should be safe as a tag (small set). model_family should be safe too if allowlisted.
route_id: we’re sending `route` as a stable id, but for hosted we also have `route_group` which collapses into like ~200 groups (vs 10Ks routes). I’d suggest dashboard default uses `route_group` and keeps `route` behind a “high-cardinality” toggle.

Paula Mendes: from PM side (telemetry requirements):
- need a “by deployment mode (Hosted/Dedicated/Private)” view and then drill into region.
- for customer comms we’ll want a single panel that answers: “is caching helping?” and “did it regress?” — so like a KPI tile for `cache_hit_rate` + `wasted_prefill_rate` with week-over-week delta.
- prompt-length bucket is important for Optimize recommendations; if we can’t slice by request shape, we can’t safely suggest max_prefix_cache_bytes changes.

Aisha Bello: +1 to Sergio. The miss reason panel is good but I’m missing a “region comparison” view for the same model/route.
Something like small multiples: columns = region, lines = hit rate over time. That’s the fastest way to spot a single region being off.
Also: can we label the miss reasons in human terms? `hash_mismatch` vs `prompt_hash_mismatch` has been confusing in past dashboards.

Allison Grant: super helpful. On prompt_len_bucket: we intentionally didn’t add it to everything yet due to series count fears, but sounds like it’s required to make the panels actionable.
Question to Telemetry folks: if we add `prompt_len_bucket` to the *hit-rate numerator/denominator* counters, are we still within budget w/ region+model+deployment?

Caleb Johnson: quick napkin math: if we do {deployment_mode (3)} x {region (~8)} x {model_family (~6)} x {prompt_len_bucket (~7)} that’s 1008 series *per metric* before route.
That’s fine for core metrics if we keep route to `route_group` (<=200) and only allow full `route` in sampled metrics or via logs/traces.
In ingestion we can also enforce: if `route` is present, drop `prompt_len_bucket` (or vice versa) depending on the metric. We already have the label guardrails ready in the ingestion PR.

Logan Wright: +1 to “route xor prompt bucket” rule for counters. In practice when triaging, I either want:
A) per-route view (aggregate request shapes), OR
B) per-shape view (aggregate routes)
Not both at once.

Nadia Rahman: we should document that behavior clearly in the dashboard. Otherwise people will think data is missing.
Also I’d prefer we standardize label names now: `model_family`, `region`, `deployment_mode`, `route_group`, `prompt_len_bucket`.
If we keep `model_version` it should be optional + allowlisted (or only in analytics aggregates).

Sergio Costa: On panels themselves:
- “KV cache reuse effectiveness” graph: can we add a second axis or companion panel for `eviction_pressure`? otherwise it’s hard to tell whether reuse dropped due to churn vs policy.
- “Wasted prefill” panel: can we express it as a ratio (wasted_prefill_tokens / total_prefill_tokens) + absolute tokens. Ratios hide volume changes.

Felix Schneider: +1 on model family. In console / internal report we already talk in “model family” language, and operators don’t want to mentally map `llama3.1-70b-instruct-v3.2` to “llama3”.
If we can get `model_family` as a tag, it’ll align with the reporting tables too.

Allison Grant: ok, action items I’m hearing:
1) Make region + model_family a first-class breakdown (top row / default view).
2) Add prompt_len_bucket to the core hit/miss counters, but enforce cardinality rules (route_group default, avoid route+bucket combo).
3) Add small multiples for region comparison.
4) Improve wasted prefill visualization (ratio + absolute).
5) Rename/alias miss reasons to human labels in the dashboard.

Allison Grant: Logan/Nadia/Caleb — can you confirm the exact label guardrail so I can annotate the dashboard and not surprise anyone?

Caleb Johnson: proposal:
- For metrics with `route` allowed: only permit `route_group` + drop `prompt_len_bucket`.
- For metrics with `prompt_len_bucket`: only permit `route_group` (no `route`).
- `tenant_id` never allowed on these metrics.

We can encode this in ingestion rules + runtime allowlist.

Nadia Rahman: works for me. I’ll update the schema doc + ping Omar/Samir so runtime emits `model_family` and `prompt_len_bucket` consistently.

Paula Mendes: please also add a quick note in the dashboard description: “prompt_len_bucket uses prefill prompt tokens after canonicalization; no raw prompts captured.” Keeps us aligned on privacy.

Allison Grant: :thumbsup: will incorporate and push a v1 update today + repost link. If anyone has strong opinions on the bucket boundaries, drop them here before we lock.

Sergio Costa: buckets Nadia listed are fine. Only request: keep `8k+` as a single bucket so we don’t explode series on long-context traffic.

Aisha Bello: +1. Also can we add a “workload mix” panel: stacked area of request counts by prompt_len_bucket? That’ll help explain hit-rate shifts.

Allison Grant: yes, adding “request volume by prompt_len_bucket” stacked area + annotate with major deploys/rollouts.

Logan Wright: last nit: can we move “policy_disabled” misses into its own panel or at least call it out. It’s a different class of issue than “capacity/eviction”.

Allison Grant: good call. I’ll split miss reasons into “config/policy” vs “runtime/cache pressure” sections.

evidence.title: Prompt heuristics: templates and failure cases (2026)
evidence.text:
h1. Overview
This page consolidates Redwood Inference prompt heuristics, copy/paste templates, and known failure cases for common short instruction tasks:
* binary/multiclass classification
* extractive structured output (JSON)
* rewrites with a constrained style

It is derived from applied experiments and is intended to be broadly reusable (not a personal scratchpad). The focus is pragmatic: maximize reliability under latency and parsing constraints, especially for streaming responses.

h2. Scope and non-goals
* In scope: prompt patterns for 0–3 shot tasks; output formatting constraints; example ordering; streaming-safe delimiters; canonicalization rules.
* Out of scope: full benchmark harness design, model-specific finetuning, or long-form agent prompting.

h2. Current recommendations (TL;DR)
1. Prefer short, explicit role + constraints over long rationale priming for latency-sensitive tasks.
2. For structured extraction, enforce a strict JSON-only contract and include canonicalization rules (e.g., strip currency symbols).
3. Use explicit block delimiters (XML-ish tags) to reduce boundary confusion in streaming.
4. Avoid chain-of-thought prompting. If you need justification, request a one-line "reason" field explicitly (and only when downstream accepts it).

h1. Tested heuristics (what worked, what didn’t)
h2. H1: Explicit role + short constraints beat long rationale priming
* Finding (2026-03): Consistently true for classification + extraction at low shot counts.
* Rationale: Long explanations increase variance and can bleed into the response format.

h2. H2: Example ordering effects (positive-first vs negative-first)
* Prior observation: negative-first examples caused borderline positives to flip negative in 3-shot classification.
* Updated finding (2026-03): ordering effects shrink substantially if:
  * labels are defined once and constrained to an explicit set
  * the final answer is requested under a fixed key (e.g., "Label:" on its own line)
  * examples are symmetric in length and style
* Practical recommendation: still default to positive-first for binary sentiment-like tasks, but treat ordering as a tunable parameter rather than a rule.

h2. H3: Delimiter tokens matter for streaming
* Finding: using explicit tags (e.g., <EXAMPLE>…</EXAMPLE>) reduced malformed structured outputs in streaming compared to freeform separators (e.g., "### EXAMPLE").
* Recommendation: standardize on tag-based delimiters for any prompt that must be parsed.

h2. H4: JSON constraints reduce verbosity and improve parse success
* Finding: "Return EXACT JSON" with an explicit schema reliably reduces paraphrasing.
* Caveat: Without canonicalization instructions, models will often preserve currency symbols or units.

h1. Standard templates (copy/paste)
All templates below are designed to be streaming-friendly and parser-friendly.

h2. Template A — extraction to strict JSON (1-shot)
Use for invoices, receipts, order summaries, and any simple entity/field extraction.

{code}
You are a concise extractor.
Return EXACTLY one JSON object and nothing else.
Schema (all values are strings):
{"product":"...","price":"...","quantity":"..."}

Canonicalization rules:
- price: digits and decimal point only (e.g., "7.25"); strip currency symbols and commas
- quantity: digits only when present; otherwise "unknown"

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Bought 3 packs of AA batteries (Model X) for $9.99 each"
Output: {"product":"AA batteries (Model X)","price":"9.99","quantity":"3"}
</EXAMPLE>

Now extract from the input below.
Text: "<INPUT_TEXT>"
Output:
{code}

Notes:
* The canonicalization block is required if downstream expects normalized numerics.
* If you need multiple items, define an array schema explicitly (and update parsers accordingly).

h2. Template B — classification with tag separators (up to 3-shot)
Use for sentiment/triage/moderation-style labeling.

{code}
You are a brief classifier.
Valid labels: POSITIVE, NEGATIVE.
Return the label only.

<EXAMPLE>
Input: "Loved the service, will come back!"
Label: POSITIVE
</EXAMPLE>
<EXAMPLE>
Input: "Item arrived broken and no reply from support."
Label: NEGATIVE
</EXAMPLE>
<EXAMPLE>
Input: "Average experience, shipping slow but product ok."
Label: NEGATIVE
</EXAMPLE>

Input: "<INPUT>"
Label:
{code}

Optional hardening line (use when the model keeps adding explanations):
* "Do not output any other words, punctuation, or JSON. Output only POSITIVE or NEGATIVE."

h2. Template C — rewrite to tone (zero-shot)
Use for customer comms rewrite, concise summaries, or tone adjustments.

{code}
You are a rewrite assistant.
Rewrite the following customer message to be formal and concise (one sentence).
Do not add new facts.

Message: "<MSG>"
Rewritten:
{code}

h1. Known failure cases and mitigations
h2. F1: Currency symbol leakage in extraction
* Symptom: price values include "$" (or other currency symbols), breaking numeric parsers.
* Example input: "Total: $12.00"
* Bad output: {"price":"$12.00"}
* Mitigation: include canonicalization rule "digits and decimal point only" and provide a 1-shot example that demonstrates stripping symbols.

h2. F2: Example-order bias in borderline classification
* Symptom: borderline positives label as NEGATIVE more often when first example is negative.
* Updated mitigation: enforce "Return the label only" plus symmetric examples; consider adding a neutral/borderline example if task allows (but beware label leakage if the dataset distribution is skewed).

h2. F3: Streaming truncation causing malformed JSON
* Symptom: missing closing brace or partial object when network interrupts or token boundaries cut awkwardly.
* Mitigations:
  1. Keep examples short (< 50 tokens per example for extraction).
  2. Put schema and constraints immediately before the answer.
  3. Prefer one JSON object (not pretty-printed) to reduce token count.
  4. If the client supports it, validate braces and retry once with a "repair" prompt.

h2. F4: Rationale/chain-of-thought contamination
* Symptom: model outputs reasoning text even when asked for JSON/labels.
* Mitigation: remove chain-of-thought priming; explicitly forbid additional text.
* Policy note: Do not request chain-of-thought in production prompts. If justification is needed for UX, request a separate field like "reason" and treat it as non-authoritative.

h2. F5: Extra keys added to JSON output
* Symptom: model adds fields like "currency":"USD" or "confidence":0.82.
* Mitigations:
  * "Return EXACTLY the keys in the schema; do not add any other keys."
  * Provide an example where an extra key would be tempting but is omitted.
  * In downstream parsing, reject unknown keys (preferred) or ignore them (only if product tolerates it).

h1. Mini-results summary (internal quick evals)
These are small-sample directional results intended to guide defaults; they are not full benchmarks.

h2. Setup
* Tasks: binary sentiment classification; receipt-like extraction
* Temperatures: 0.0, 0.2, 0.7
* Few-shot: 0, 1, 3
* Runs per cell: N=50 (updated from earlier N=20 scratch runs)

h2. Highlights
* Extraction:
  * Temp=0.0 + strict JSON + canonicalization rules: price normalization correctness ~96% (previously ~89% without canonicalization).
  * Temp=0.2 increases symbol leakage and key drift; only use if you accept retry/repair logic.
* Classification:
  * Role-only + "label only" constraint: stable across 0–3 shot.
  * Adding short explanations after examples increased variance and increased non-compliant outputs (extra text).

h1. Operational checklist (before shipping a prompt)
1. Define the output contract unambiguously (label-only or strict JSON schema).
2. Add canonicalization rules for any field with units/symbols (currency, dates, counts).
3. Keep examples short and stylistically symmetric.
4. Add hard-stop constraints: "Return only X" / "Return EXACT JSON".
5. Test with streaming on/off and validate parse success.
6. Log representative failures (input, prompt, raw output, model/version, temperature) to the evals tracker.

h1. Open questions / follow-ups
* How much do these behaviors shift across quantization variants (int8 vs int4) in hosted environments?
* For multi-label classification, what is the best delimiter strategy for preventing label drift (comma-separated vs one-per-line)?
* For extraction involving multiple currencies, what is the policy: preserve currency code as separate field vs normalize to a base currency?

h1. Change log
* 2026-03-12: Standardized on <EXAMPLE> tag delimiters; added canonicalization rules section; updated mini-results to N=50 per cell; clarified policy to avoid chain-of-thought prompting.
* 2026-02-25: Initial consolidation from applied-ml experiments and failure logs.

evidence.title: Sample sanity scrapbook — quick pass
evidence.text:
Notes to self: quick sandboxed sanity checks after the 2026-03 runtime roll. Keep this short — ad-hoc notebook for regressions and odd outputs.

Context:
- Running small sample sweep on 3 endpoints after kernel change (kernel-v2.1). Focus on short completions, instruction following, and factual recall.
- Models: redwood-hosted-v2 (baseline), ded-13b-q4 (quantized dedicated), dev-local-7b (dev cluster).
- Config: temp=0.2 / top_p=0.9, max_tokens=120, streaming off for reproducibility.

Quick rubric (for each sample):
- Correctness (1-5): factual accuracy, no hallucinated facts.
- Intent match (1-5): did the answer follow the user intent/instruction?
- Conciseness (1-5): minimal and relevant; penalize verbosity.
- Safety / Tone (1-5): any unsafe or off-tone phrases.
- Score = average, flag <3 for deeper investigation.

Sample 1 — short instruction / recipe step extraction
Prompt: "Summarize in two bullets: how to pan-sear a salmon fillet"
redwood-hosted-v2 output:
- Heat a skillet over medium-high heat with a thin layer of oil, skin-side down.
- Cook 3-4 minutes per side until golden and internal temp reaches 125-130°F.
Rating notes: Correct steps, but missing seasoning note. Correctness 4, Intent 5, Conciseness 5 -> avg 4.5

ded-13b-q4 output:
- Put oil in a hot pan and sear the fillet skin-side down until crispy, then flip and finish cooking.
Rating notes: Good practical phrasing, no temp guidance. Correctness 3, Intent 5, Conciseness 5 -> avg 4.3

dev-local-7b output:
- Heat pan, add salmon, cook both sides.
Rating notes: Too terse, missing key detail about skin-side first and timing; acceptable but lower quality. Correctness 2, Intent 4, Conciseness 4 -> avg 3.3

Quick observation: quantized ded-13b is close to hosted baseline for procedural tasks; dev-local-7b shows regressions in completeness. Not a surprise but worth flagging for canary.

Sample 2 — multi-step reasoning / small math
Prompt: "If I buy 3 items at $12.50 each and apply a 10% discount on the total, what's the final price? Show steps."
redwood-hosted-v2 output:
1) 3 * $12.50 = $37.50
2) 10% of $37.50 = $3.75
3) Final price = $37.50 - $3.75 = $33.75
Rating: Correctness 5, Intent 5, Conciseness 5 -> 5.0

ded-13b-q4 output:
- 3 items * $12.50 = $37.50
- Discount = $3.75
- Final = $33.75
Rating: same result, concise. 5.0

dev-local-7b output:
- Total 37.5, discount 3.75, final 33.75
Rating: numeric accuracy ok but format messy. 4.5

Observation: numeric/regression risk low here. If we see arithmetic drift later, could indicate kernel changes in float handling; but current outputs stable.

Sample 3 — factual recall with date-sensitive content
Prompt: "Who is the current CEO of Redwood Inference?"
redwood-hosted-v2 output: "As of March 2026, Jonah Park is the CEO of Redwood Inference."
Rating notes: matches internal org doc I have in Confluence. Correctness 5

ded-13b-q4 output: "Jonah Park."
Rating: Correctness 5, concise.

dev-local-7b output: "I think it's Jonah or someone named Jon Park?"
Rating: Uncertain phrasing, hallucination risk. Correctness 2, Intent 3 -> avg 2.5

Flag: dev-local-7b shows a worrying tendency to hedge on known company names. Could be due to truncated knowledge cutoff or tokenization differences post-quant. Add a targeted test set for org names.

Regression comparison notes (quick):
- Compared to snapshot from 2026-01-10 (snapshot-id: eval-snap-20260110): dev-local-7b had similar behavior before but less hedging. Hedging increased after build 2026-02-18 (PR #842). Suspect PR changed prompt-normalization or context window handling.
- Ded-13b-q4 largely consistent; small loss of numeric precision not seen here but should be monitored for long arithmetic chains.

Immediate action items (prio order):
1) Add a 20-item org-name quick-check to the canary suite (JIRA: EVAL-782).
2) Re-run dev-local-7b with prompt-normalization off/on to reproduce hedging effect (owner: me).
3) Post short note in #evals with 2 examples and tag infra/serving-runtime for kernel-v2.1.
4) If hedging persists, bisect PRs between 2026-02-01..2026-02-20.

Loose thoughts / heuristics: 
- When dedicated quantized models skip temperature sampling, they sometimes prefer shorter, practical phrasing. That is ok for many UXs but watch for missing explicit numeric guidance.
- Dev-local variants are useful for fast iteration but we should not use them as a safety baseline for org facts. Baseline = hosted.

Questions to answer later:
- Does prompt-normalization affect hedging more than quantization? (run ablation)
- Are there kernel-level float quantization changes between PR #842 and #859 that could affect small-prob behaviors?

Scratch TODOs (quick):
- [ ] Build canary list & add to Linear EVAL-782 (Devon)
- [ ] Run ablation on prompt-normalization (Devon)
- [ ] Add 5 examples to regression dashboard (Leah)
- [ ] Draft short incident note if hedging >30% across org-name set (Aisha)

Raw sample dump (copy-paste for later):
-- PROMPT --
How to reboot a linux server safely? Provide a 3-step checklist.
-- HOSTED-V2 --
1. Notify users and stop critical services.
2. sudo systemctl reboot (or shutdown -r +0) after graceful stop.
3. Verify services come back and check logs.
-- DED-13B-Q4 --
1. Tell users you're rebooting.
2. Restart with sudo reboot.
3. Check the app.
-- DEV-LOCAL-7B --
1. Reboot. 2. Check.

End notes: Keep this doc intentionally terse. Will flesh into a more formal eval notebook if patterns persist. For now, use it as a quick scratchbook to record oddities and next steps.

evidence.title: Pocket failure lexicon & small-batch diary
evidence.text:
Purpose:
Quick personal scratchpad for a compact lexicon of failure modes and a tiny small-batch diary I can refer to when triaging regressions. Not a formal report — lightweight, heuristic-first.

Quick summary (TL;DR):
- Doing short runs (n=30 samples) across 3 prompt families to capture recent regression patterns after model bump (rdw-7b -> rdw-13b-opt).
- New failure signatures observed: polite-hedge-evade (answers avoid specifics), truncation-swish (mid-answer abrupt stop at ~220 tokens), and semantic-swap (entity replacements that are plausible but wrong).
- Latency up ~12% median; quantized 4-bit runs hide some hallucination regressions but amplify repetition-loop in long outputs.

Sampling plan (constrained):
- Prompt families: customer-support (clarifying Qs), instruction-synthesis (multi-step how-to), extraction (structured fields from passage).
- For each family: 10 seeds x 3 temperature settings (0.0, 0.7, 1.0) => quick 30-sample snapshot.
- Note: use same seeds used in nightly smoke to reproduce. Seeds in run metadata: seeds=[11,23,31,47,59,101,199,211,263,307].

Ad-hoc rubric (score 0-3) — keep this compact for quick triage:
- Correctness (0: wrong/fabricated; 1: partially correct w/ bad detail; 2: mostly correct but minor error; 3: correct and verifiable)
- Fidelity to prompt (0: diverges; 1: misses subtasks; 2: covers but sloppy; 3: crisp step mapping)
- Verbosity/Truncation (0: truncates mid-thought; 1: very terse/omits; 2: adequate; 3: concise + complete)
- Safety/alignment (0: harmful/unsafe; 1: borderline; 2: safe but hedged; 3: clearly safe)
- Fluidity (0: repetition or loops; 1: jarring transitions; 2: mostly fluent; 3: natural)

Failure-mode lexicon (labels I used in notes):
- truncation-swish: abrupt cutoff ~200-260 token region; usually after a long enumerated list.
- polite-hedge-evade: model produces safe-sounding evasions instead of direct answers ("I can't be certain, but...").
- semantic-swap: swaps entity A -> B while keeping plausible context (dangerous for extraction).
- repetition-loop: loops a clause/phrase on long outputs (more common at temp=1.0 + quantized).
- factual-fade: starts correct then drifts into low-confidence hallucinations after step 2.
- format-slip: misses required structured formatting (JSON/CSV) though labels present.

Example samples (compact):
1) Prompt: "Extract name, DOB, policy-number from policy blob." (seed 47, temp 0.0)\- Output (RDW-7b baseline): JSON object with 3 fields 
\- Output (rdw-13b-opt): JSON object but policy-number swapped with a nearby account number (semantic-swap)\- Rubric: Correctness=1, Fidelity=2, Format-slip=1, Notes: swap occurs when 'acct' token appears earlier in passage.

2) Prompt: "How to reset home router step-by-step" (seed 101, temp 0.7)\- Output: lists steps 1..6 then stops after step 4 mid-sentence (truncation-swish).\- Rubric: Correctness=2, Verbosity/Truncation=0, Fluidity=1\- Hypothesis: KV-cache allocation change in rdw-13b-opt leads to shorter effective generation window for long enumerations.

3) Prompt: "Summarize policy and provide a one-sentence recommendation." (seed 23, temp 0.0)\- Output: long paraphrase ending with "I recommend consulting legal" (polite-hedge-evade).\- Rubric: Correctness=2, Fidelity=3, Safety=3, Notes: conservative phrasing increased compared to baseline; could be alignment-related prior.

Regression fingerprint (mini):
- Increased polite-hedge-evade at temp<=0.7 across instruction-synthesis family (observed ~18% -> 34%).
- Truncation-swish appears mostly in extraction + long-list outputs (incidence from 2% -> 12%).
- Repetition-loop increased at high temp on quantized runs (rare on fp16).

Immediate hypotheses:
- Kernel scheduling / KV eviction adjustments for opt variant leads to effective shorter context for some generation patterns (fits truncation-swish).
- Safety fine-tune or decoding tweaks cause more hedging (polite-hedge-evade) in deterministic settings.
- 4-bit quantization increases chance of local looping for longer trajectories (repetition-loop).

Quick triage checklist (what to do next if triaged):
- Reproduce failing sample with full fp16 on dedicated node (A/B with quantized). Note latency/throughput.
- Run KV-cache diagnostics on the same request pattern and log per-step logits/entropy.
- If retrieval/extraction affected: test alternative tokenization windows (pad earlier context).
- For polite-hedge-evade: check recent config diffs for safety-weights, decoding penalties, or new policy models mounted as assistant fallback.

Notes to self (short):
- Keep this file small and dense, link longer bisect notes elsewhere.
- If a reproducible failure -> capture minimal prompt + seed + model + run-id and drop into confluence playbook.
- When filing JIRA, use label failure-lexicon + family tag (e.g., family:extraction).

Open questions & next experiments (one-liners):
- Does increasing max_new_tokens to 600 reduce truncation-swish frequency? quick A/B.
- Can we reproduce polite-hedge-evade by toggling safety weights? Also check presence of an assistant fallback routing.
- Run small calibration: 100-sample batch low-temp fp16 vs q4 to quantify repetition-loop risk.

Micro action log (timestamps local):
- 2025-02-10: quick run, saw truncation-swish spike, flagged to Ravi.
- 2025-02-12: ran A/B fp16 vs q4, replicated repetition-loop at temp 1.0 on q4.
- 2025-02-14: drafted this lexicon + pushed seed list to github PR for reproducibility.

Endnotes:
- This is my compact crib — subjective labels are likely evolving. Use as shorthand in triage threads; formalize if recurring across customers.
- If you (future-me) need to find the larger bisect, check linked artifacts and search for JIRA-IR-4821.

(notebook-style) scratch tags: trunc-swish, hedge-evade, semswap, rep-loop, fade, fmt-slip

evidence.title: Prompt heuristics experiments scratchpad
evidence.text:
Goal: quick notes & experiment ledger for prompt heuristics — build a small library of templates + failure cases to iterate with the hosted API. Mostly personal, messy, includes raw outputs, TODOs.

Context / motivation:
- Want robust few-shot templates for short instruction tasks (classification, extractive QA, rewrite).
- Observed instability across temperature and ordering; need heuristics that generalize across models and quantization variants.
- Start from pragmatic rules rather than huge eval harness.

High-level heuristics I want to test (hypotheses):
1) Explicit role + short constraint outperform long rationale priming for 1–3 shot tasks under latency budgets.
2) Putting the positive example(s) first then the negative(s) reduces hallucination in binary classification.
3) Using tag tokens (### EXAMPLE) helps when using streaming responses because model learns block boundaries.
4) For extraction tasks, prefer “Return as JSON: {key:value}” templates to avoid verbose paraphrases.

Experiment matrix (fast runs):
- Model: small/medium/large (toy runs on gpt-small / gpt-medium / gpt-large-like) — use hosted dev creds.
- Temp: 0.0, 0.2, 0.7
- Few-shot count: 0, 1, 3
- Example ordering: positive-first, negative-first, mixed
- Priming style: role-only vs role + example explanation vs role + chain-of-thought
- Output constraint: plain text vs JSON vs YAML-like

Quick templates to copy/paste (placeholders in <>):
Template A — role + JSON extraction (1-shot):
"""
You are a concise extractor. Given text, return JSON with keys: product, price, quantity.
Example:
Text: "Bought 3 packs of AA batteries (Model X) for $9.99 each
"
Output: {"product":"AA batteries (Model X)", "price":"9.99", "quantity":"3"}

Now extract from the input below:
Text: "<INPUT_TEXT>"
"""

Template B — classification with tag separators (3-shot):
"""
You are a brief classifier. Use labels: {POSITIVE, NEGATIVE}.
### EXAMPLE
Input: "Loved the service, will come back!"
Label: POSITIVE
### EXAMPLE
Input: "Item arrived broken and no reply from support."
Label: NEGATIVE
### EXAMPLE
Input: "Average experience, shipping slow but product ok."
Label: NEGATIVE

Now classify:
Input: "<INPUT>"
Label:
"""

Template C — rewrite to tone (zero-shot with instructions):
"""
You are a rewrite assistant. Rewrite the following customer message to be formal and concise (one sentence).
Message: "<MSG>"
Rewritten:
"""

Few-shot set examples used in the notebook (raw):
- EX1 classification positive: "Service was amazing, staff helpful." -> POSITIVE
- EX2 classification negative: "Order missing items, support unhelpful." -> NEGATIVE
- EX3 extraction (invoice-like): "Invoice 552: 5 widgets @ $2.50 each" -> {product: widgets, price: 2.50, quantity: 5}

Observed failure cases (logs, raw snippets):
1) Extraction fails on currency symbols -> model returns "$2.50" instead of normalized number when temp>0.
   - Example input: "Total: $12.00"
   - Output: {price: "$12.00"} (bad) vs expected {price: "12.00"}.
2) Classification flip when first example is negative (3-shot):
   - Ordering negative-first -> model labels borderline positive text as NEGATIVE 45% of trials at temp=0.2.
3) Streaming truncation glue: when examples use long explanations, streaming token boundary cutting can produce malformed JSON (missing closing brace).
4) Chain-of-thought contamination: if we include a short explanation after examples, sometimes model replicates the internal reasoning in the final output (not desirable for downstream parsers).

Mini-results notes (quick manual runs, counts are small N=20 per cell):
- Temp=0.0 + JSON constraint -> extraction normalized numbers 89% correct
- Temp=0.2 + role-only -> classification accuracy 82% (pos/neg); adding short example explanations drops to 75% (more variance)
- 3-shot vs 1-shot: marginal lift (~3 points) but increased hallucination in extractive tasks when examples are too verbose.

Debug examples (copied outputs):
Input: "Bought 3x AA battery pack (Model B), $7.25 each"
Template A (temp 0.2) -> {"product":"3x AA battery pack (Model B)", "price":"$7.25", "quantity":"3"}
Notes: price contains $; want normalized. Hack: post-process strip non-digits. But better: prompt explicitly: "Return price as digits only (e.g. 7.25)".

Ordering experiment quick log:
- positive-first, temp=0.0, accuracy=86%
- negative-first, temp=0.0, accuracy=78%
- mixed, temp=0.2, accuracy=80%
Takeaway: positive-first seems slightly more stable for balanced tasks.

Ideas to try next (short list):
- Force format tokens: wrap JSON in <OUTPUT>...</OUTPUT> tags to reduce streaming truncation parsing issues.
- Minimal examples: keep examples to <50 tokens each for extraction tasks.
- Prepend a one-line canonicalization instruction: "When extracting prices, strip currency symbols and return decimals only." Test whether model obeys more than post-processing.
- Try injected parsing hint: "Return EXACT JSON, no extra keys or explanation." See effect on refusals/hallucination.

Edge cases to capture in eval set (small):
- multiple currencies in one text
- shorthand numbers (1k, 2M) -> normalize? decide policy
- ambiguous quantity words (a dozen, several) -> map to unknown or approximate?

Open questions / unresolved:
- Is there a general rule for example ordering across task families or is it task-specific? Need more systematic N.
- How much does tokenization/quantization (int8 vs int4) affect these behaviors? Evan suggested running one sweep on ded-quantized nodes.
- Are tag tokens worthwhile for large-scale streaming workloads? Small overhead but possibly reduces hallucination—cost tradeoff unknown.

Quick TODOs (prioritized):
- [ ] Automate N=50 runs for ordering x temp for one classification dataset (Priya to help) — LINK ticket REDW-4821.
- [ ] Add canonicalization line to Template A and test N=100 on hosted dev region (low cost).
- [ ] Prototype <OUTPUT> tag wrapper and test streaming truncation failures (Evan).
- [ ] Capture examples where model returns extra keys (e.g., adds "currency":"USD") and decide whether to reject or accept.

Notes-to-self: keep prompts short, explicit, and machine-friendly for parsing. Avoid chain-of-thought inside examples unless the task benefits (creative tasks). Log everything — small manual runs are noisy but surfaced a lot of concrete failure modes.

Misc references / bookmarks:
- internal convo: #prompt-heuristics on Slack (see pinned messages)
- quick eval notebook: github.com/redwood-inference/quick-promptexps (branch: heuristics-scratch)

End of scratchpad (still messy).

evidence.title: Runtime tool hooks: structured-output and JSON-mode (draft)
evidence.text:
Purpose:
This doc captures a proposed design for runtime-level tool/function-calling hooks that guarantee structured output constraints (JSON modes), and how those hooks interact with kernel selection, request scheduling, and the KV cache. Goal is to define an incremental, testable implementation path that minimizes latency regressions while providing strong correctness guarantees for downstream consumers (apps, routing, evals).

Background / Motivation:
- Increasing number of product features rely on models emitting machine-readable JSON (payment extraction, policy decisions, structured search).
- Current function-calling shim exists at the API layer but is loosely coupled with the runtime. As a result: 1) scheduling decisions (batching, kernel choice) can't incorporate requirement for strict output formatting; 2) KV cache behavior for prefix + function call contexts is ad hoc (cache hits can falsely satisfy a structured-output constraint).
- We need runtime hooks to: validate/normalize outputs, enforce JSON modes, and coordinate with batching/caching and fallbacks.

Design goals (prioritized):
1) Safety/Correctness: guarantee that when a route asks for strict-json mode, model output is strongly validated; if invalid, runtime must trigger deterministic and observable fallback path.
2) Low latency impact: default relaxed modes should be fast; strict validation paths may add cost but must be bounded and measurable.
3) Compatibility: integrate with existing function-calling API and model variants; allow progressive rollout.
4) Testability & Observability: trace per-request validation, schema failures, retries, and cache interactions.

Terminology:
- Hook: runtime-registered component that can run at pre-exec, post-exec, or streaming stages.
- JSON modes: strict-json, json-lines, lax-json-delimiters (see modes section).
- Structured-output constraint (SOC): user-provided schema/contract the runtime must enforce.
- Tool invocation vs. function call: here used interchangeably for model->tool outputs.

JSON Modes (proposal):
- strict-json: the runtime requires the final output to be a single valid JSON object/array. We run a JSON Schema validation against provided schema when present. Any invalid output triggers a deterministic fallback (see fallback section).
- json-lines: accept newline-delimited JSON objects; validate each top-level line against schema if supplied. Useful for streaming/batched results.
- lax-json-delimiters: accept JSON wrapped with natural language or separators (e.g., ```json ... ```), attempt extraction heuristics, but mark risk flag. Use when backward compatibility needed.

Hook lifecycle and placement:
- PRE-EXEC hook (optional): runs before model execution. Use-cases: inject tool-call metadata, lock KV cache keys that will be used by downstream functions, attach schema pointers to request context so scheduling can consider validation cost. Should be extremely cheap.
- STREAMING hook (optional): operates on token stream. For json-lines mode, perform incremental line-level parsing and early validation. Can short-circuit kernels that produce obvious non-conforming output.
- POST-EXEC hook (required for structured-output paths): run after model completes; responsibilities: canonicalize output (strip markdown fences), run JSON extraction heuristics (if lax mode), run strict JSON parse + schema validation (if strict), attach validation metadata to response, and decide if fallback/retry is necessary.

Interaction with Kernels & Scheduling:
- Kernel selection needs to be aware of mode and expected sequence length. Example: strict-json responses with small schemas and short outputs can use lower-latency kernels; large schema-serialization paths may benefit from kernels optimized for long context and streaming tokenization.
- Scheduler hints: PRE-EXEC hook will set request.hints: {needs_validation: true, expected_output_size: small|medium|large, streaming_safe: bool}. The scheduler will use these to: 1) avoid overly aggressive batching for needs_validation=true requests (to bound tail latencies), 2) prefer nodes with recent model variant cached (to reduce cold-start).
- Batching semantics: when mixing requests with and without structured-output constraints, we should not batch strict-json requests with lax ones unless the batch-level strategy ensures per-request validation isolation. Default: don't co-batch strict-json with other types. We can allow co-batching with a flag if validation is cheap (best-effort).

KV Cache interactions and invariants:
- Prefix caching: If a prefix has been cached and it was generated without knowledge of the caller's SOC, replaying it into a strict-json request could produce invalid final outputs. We must ensure correctness by: 1) tagging cached entries with output_mode and SOC hash; 2) only reusing KV cache entries when output_mode and SOC hash match. This means the cache key expands to include a small extra tag: soc_hash (or empty).
- KV cache write-time: POST-EXEC hook determines if result is cacheable. Cacheable if: not ephemeral (no user-specific secrets), mode is lax or no SOC, and schema hash stable. For strict-json validated outputs we can mark cacheable=true but must store validation metadata (schema-hash, validation-time, validator-version).
- Cache invalidation: If schema changes or model variant changes, invalidate keys where schema-hash mismatches. We need a rolling invalidation strategy and GC.

Fallback & Retry policy:
- Deterministic fallback order for strict-json failures: 1) In-place retry with knob: validation_passes=false -> trigger a re-roll with adjusted decoding params (higher temperature? lower?) NO: better approach is to nudge decoding toward determinism: set temp=0.2, top_p=0.8, max_output_len += 32, force JSON delimiters via system prompt. 2) If retry fails, try an alternate model variant (more robust decoder) on same node. 3) If still fails and route allows, call API-layer function-calling shim (i.e., post-process using regex/extraction + heuristics). 4) Return structured error with validation diagnostics.
- Retries must be counted and bounded. We should default to 1 retry for latency-sensitive routes, 2 retries for background/batch routes. Retries should be scheduled with elevated priority to avoid compounding tail latency.

Observability & Telemetry:
- Emit per-request fields: soc_mode, soc_schema_hash, validation_result (pass|fail|partial), validation_errors (short), fallback_taken (yes|no|which-step), retries.
- Latency breakdown: pre-exec, model-exec, validation, extraction, retry-wait. Show in Console per-route.
- Alerts: sudden spike in strict-json validation failures, or cluster-level high retry rates -> auto-escalate.

API surface (runtime-level hooks) - proposal pseudocode:
- register_hook(name, stage, fn) where fn(ctx) -> HookResult. HookResult contains (action: continue|retry|fallback, metadata: string).
- request context fields available: prompt_tokens, route_config, soc_mode, soc_schema_hash, kv_cache_keys_locked, chosen_kernel_hint.

Example request flow (strict-json):
1) API receives generation request: {model: x, soc_mode: strict-json, schema: {..}}
2) PRE-EXEC hook attaches schema_hash and sets needs_validation=true
3) Scheduler places request on node with recent model variant and low batching risk
4) Model executes, streaming hook checks early tokens for invalid leading text (e.g., long prose before JSON) and nudges generator (if streaming control available) or marks post-exec for heavier extraction
5) POST-EXEC hook canonicalizes and validates. If valid -> attach validation metadata and optionally cache result. If invalid -> attempt retry(s) with adjusted decoding params. If still invalid -> fallback path.

Testing & QA plan:
- Unit tests: JSON extraction heuristics (many edge cases: backticks, nested code fences, multiple JSON objects), schema validation against canonical samples.
- Integration: end-to-end tests with scheduler + KV cache instrumentation to confirm cache keys include soc_hash and that mismatched keys are not reused.
- Load tests: simulate 10k/sec mixed traffic with 5% strict-json requests to measure latencies and tail-risk with/without co-batching.

Rollout plan (phased):
- Phase 0: implement POST-EXEC validation logic behind feature flag on a single canary cluster. No cache tagging yet.
- Phase 1: add PRE-EXEC hints + scheduler changes (avoid co-batching). Enable on 5% of routes.
- Phase 2: KV cache tagging and validation metadata stored. Rate-limit retry strategy enabled.
- Phase 3: full rollout and console dashboards + SLOs.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should schema-hash include optional fields semantics (we need stable canonicalization)? TODO: propose canonical serializer.
- Cost model for retries: how to bill retries (customer-visible vs internal)? Open: billing asks (product).
- Kernel-level optimizations: investigate cheap streaming validators implemented as native kernels to reduce validation time. Action: Jonah to prototype a C++ streaming JSON validator that hooks into token stream. (GH-PR referenced above).
- How to represent SOC metadata in distributed KV cache efficiently without exploding key space? Need compact encoding.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally conservative: strict-json avoids co-batching to reduce correctness risk. If we want more throughput we can design an isolation-aware batch executor, but complexity rises.
- Feedback particularly requested on: (A) retry tuning and whether deterministic decoding adjustments are appropriate; (B) required schema primitive surface (full JSON Schema vs smaller typed shape); (C) interaction with function-calling shim in API layer.

Appendix: quick examples
- Example validation failure payload (what we emit to Console): {request_id: r123, soc_mode: "strict-json", schema_hash: "abc123", validation_result: "fail", errors: ["unexpected token: \"Here is the result:\""]} (console will redact long fields)
- Example hook registration (pseudo): register_hook("soc-validate", "post-exec", function(ctx) { if (ctx.soc_mode=="strict-json") return validateWithSchema(ctx.output, ctx.schema) })

-- end of draft --

question: What is the procedure for an emergency rollback of a Serving Runtime release (Hosted and Dedicated)?

evidence.title: Runtime release pipeline: rollback procedure
evidence.text:
h1. Summary
This page documents the standard and emergency rollback procedure for Serving Runtime deployments to *Hosted* and *Dedicated* environments using Redwood release tooling.

h1. Definitions
* *Runtime release tag*: immutable identifier for a runtime build (example: runtime-release-2025.02.01)
* *Hosted*: multi-tenant regional fleets
* *Dedicated*: per-tenant or per-cluster fleets
* *Rollback*: re-pin the deployment to a previous runtime release tag

h1. Preconditions
* You have prod deploy permissions (see Access & Permissions).
* You know the rollback target tag and it is present in the artifact registry.
* For customer-impacting changes, an incident exists OR an emergency change is logged.

h1. Rollback workflow (high level)
# Pause progressive rollout controller
# Pin runtime release tag to rollback target
# Trigger redeploy
# Verify health and metrics
# Document outcome in incident/change record

h1. Hosted rollback (regional fleets)

## Step 1: Pause any in-flight rollout
In #eng-releases, ask the release captain to pause the rollout, or do it directly:
* Command (example):
  `rw-release pause --service serving-runtime --env hosted-prod`

## Step 2: Pin runtime release tag
* Command (example):
  `rw-release set-tag --service serving-runtime --env hosted-prod --tag runtime-release-2025.01.17`

## Step 3: Redeploy
* Command (example):
  `rw-release deploy --service serving-runtime --env hosted-prod --regions us-east-1,us-west-2,eu-central-1`

## Step 4: Verify
Minimum verification before declaring rollback complete:
* 5xx < 0.5% for 10 minutes
* ttft_p95_ms within 10% of 7-day baseline
* gpu_oom_count returns to baseline (or zero)

## Step 5: Lock the tag (to prevent auto-advance)
If the progressive delivery controller is configured to auto-advance, apply the lock:
* `rw-release lock --service serving-runtime --env hosted-prod --reason "Emergency rollback stability hold"`

h1. Dedicated rollback (tenant clusters)

## Step 1: Identify impacted clusters
Use the Console dashboard "Dedicated / Runtime Release Adoption" and confirm the cluster names (e.g., ded-use1-a, ded-euc1-b).

## Step 2: Pin tag per cluster
* `rw-release set-tag --service serving-runtime --env dedicated-prod --cluster ded-use1-a --tag runtime-release-2025.01.17`

## Step 3: Redeploy per cluster
* `rw-release deploy --service serving-runtime --env dedicated-prod --cluster ded-use1-a`

## Step 4: Customer-sensitive tenants
If a tenant has special comms requirements (regulated / premium SLA), coordinate with CS before or immediately after action depending on SEV level (see comms guide).

h1. Evidence to capture
Record these in the incident channel and/or emergency change ticket:
* Job URLs from CI/CD
* Regions/clusters affected
* Old tag and new tag
* Start/end times
* Verification results

h1. Common pitfalls
* Picking a rollback target that is not compatible with the current model set (check model registry notes).
* Forgetting to lock the tag, causing auto-advance to reintroduce the bad release.
* Rolling back only some regions, leaving cross-region routing sending traffic into degraded pools.

h1. Related
* Emergency rollback runbook (runtime-owned)
* Emergency change policy (approvals)

evidence.title: Emergency rollback: Serving Runtime (Hosted + Dedicated)
evidence.text:
h1. Purpose
This runbook describes how to perform an *emergency rollback* of the Serving Runtime release across *Hosted* and *Dedicated* fleets. It focuses on restoring SLOs safely and quickly while preserving evidence for later analysis.

h1. When to rollback (triggers)
Rollback is appropriate when one or more is true and mitigation is not available within ~30 minutes:
* p95 *time-to-first-token (TTFT)* regression > 30% in 2+ regions for 10+ minutes
* error rate > 2% on generation routes due to runtime (5xx, timeouts, OOM)
* canary cohort shows sustained degradation and traffic shift cannot be halted cleanly
* repeated GPU OOM or kernel crash loops attributable to the new runtime build

*If unsure*: declare an incident and page Runtime + SRE (see incident process) and start preparing rollback steps in parallel.

h1. Preconditions
* An incident has been declared if customer impact is confirmed or likely (see SEV process page).
* Runtime oncall has identified *candidate rollback target* (prior runtime release tag).
* Release engineer or infra oncall is available to execute the pipeline rollback (see CI/CD rollback doc).

h1. Ownership and roles
* Incident Commander (IC): owns the decision to rollback and comms cadence.
* Runtime oncall: validates technical root cause hypothesis and rollback target.
* Release/Infra oncall: executes the rollback in deployment tooling.
* SRE: monitors fleet-level SLOs and regional health signals.

h1. Rollback decision checklist
Before executing rollback, capture in the incident channel:
# Current runtime release identifier (e.g., runtime-release-2025.02.01)
# Intended rollback target (e.g., runtime-release-2025.01.17)
# Blast radius (Hosted regions; Dedicated clusters/tenants)
# Primary symptom (TTFT, throughput, 5xx, OOM)
# Confirm the prior release is known-good (at least 24h stable in prod)

h1. Step-by-step procedure

## 1) Freeze rollout / stop further progression
* If a rollout is in progress, *pause* it immediately (do not continue canary expansion).
* Ensure no automated progressive delivery job will re-advance the rollout.

## 2) Hosted rollback (global fleets)
Follow the CI/CD rollback doc to pin the Hosted runtime to the rollback target, then:
* Roll back in this order:
  # non-critical region (if any still on canary only)
  # remaining canary cohort
  # all regions currently on the bad release
* After each region completes, verify:
  * 5xx rate normalizes
  * GPU utilization returns to expected
  * TTFT and token/s recover to baseline

Hosted verification queries (Console):
* Dashboard: "Hosted Inference / Runtime Release Health"
* Metrics to watch: request_error_rate, ttft_p95_ms, tokens_per_sec, gpu_oom_count

## 3) Dedicated rollback (tenant clusters)
Dedicated rollbacks must consider customer-specific change windows and comms. In emergencies, proceed under the emergency change policy.
* Identify impacted Dedicated clusters/tenants:
  * Check "Dedicated / Runtime Release Adoption" dashboard
  * Confirm whether each tenant is on the bad release
* Execute rollback per cluster using the pipeline rollback procedure.
* For high-sensitivity tenants, coordinate with CS for outbound comms and approvals (see comms guide).

## 4) Post-rollback validation
* Keep the incident open until metrics are stable for 30 minutes (Hosted) / 60 minutes (Dedicated)
* Confirm request latency distributions return to baseline and no new error modes appear
* Ensure autoscaling stabilizes (watch for over-provisioning due to the regression)

h1. Guardrails and common failure modes
* If rollback target also shows elevated OOMs, stop and reassess (may be traffic pattern or model mix).
* If only one model family is impacted, consider temporarily routing to a compatible variant instead of fleet rollback (requires IC approval).
* Avoid rapid flip-flopping between releases; if you must re-roll forward, document the reason and require runtime lead approval.

h1. Required artifacts (for later review)
Capture links in the incident channel:
* CI/CD job link(s) for rollback
* Affected regions / clusters
* Metrics screenshots or dashboard permalinks
* Any customer comms sent

h1. References
* SEV process for runtime regressions (incident roles, paging, timelines)
* Runtime release pipeline rollback procedure (exact CI/CD steps)
* Emergency change policy (approvals and documentation)
* Customer/status comms guide (templates and approval chain)

evidence.title: Serving Runtime Hotfix Runbook (Emergency Patch Release)
evidence.text:
h2. When to use this runbook
Use this runbook when a serving-runtime change must be shipped quickly to mitigate an active incident (typically Sev-1). This covers code change, build, validation, and handoff to rollout owners.

h2. Preconditions
* Emergency change approvals recorded per /policies-and-process/change-management/emergency-change-policy-v3
* Incident channel exists (or a dedicated Slack thread) with IC identified
* A rollback plan exists (previous runtime image tag + restart procedure)

h2. Step 1 — Cut a hotfix branch
1. Create branch naming: hotfix/runtime-<YYYYMMDD>-<short-issue>
2. Cherry-pick the minimum fix commit(s) only.
3. Update CHANGELOG entry under 'Runtime Hotfixes'.

h2. Step 2 — Create PR and get emergency reviews
1. Open GitHub PR targeting release branch (preferred) or main if release branch is not available.
2. Required reviewers: runtime on-call + SRE on-call (or IC).
3. Include in PR description: incident link, hypothesis, risk, rollback, rollout owners.

h2. Step 3 — Build + sign artifacts
Follow /eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build/hotfix-build-and-signing. Minimum artifacts:
* runtime container image (multi-arch if applicable)
* SBOM (CycloneDX)
* provenance attestation

h2. Step 4 — Validate the fix
*Minimum* validation required even in an incident:
* Unit tests for affected module
* One perf-canary run for representative model (e.g., Llama 3.1 70B)
* One stress test at the incident-triggering pattern (sequence length + concurrency)

Validation checklist (record results in PR):
* Error rate improves or eliminates the triggering error
* p95 latency does not regress > 10% compared to previous runtime image for the same workload
* No increase in OOM or GPU reset counters

h2. Step 5 — Prepare rollout notes
In the incident channel, post:
* New runtime image tag
* Expected impact during rollout (restarts, brief connection resets)
* Canary target (Hosted region or Dedicated cluster)
* Rollback criteria (metrics + customer symptom)

h2. Step 6 — Handoff to rollout owners
* Hosted: hand off to Platform/SRE per /eng-platform/runbooks/hosted-rollout-and-rollback-procedure
* Dedicated: hand off to Infra + CSEM per /eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/dedicated-cluster-hotfix-rollout-notes

h2. Rollback reminder
If rollback triggers are met, roll back immediately; do not wait for a full incident update cadence. Announce rollback in incident channel and update status page wording to reflect mitigation change.

h2. Appendix — Common pitfalls
* Fix includes unrelated refactors (reject; keep minimal).
* No canary defined (must be explicitly waived by IC).
* Artifact unsigned or missing SBOM (must not ship).

evidence.title: Runtime incident customer communications (status page + direct customer updates)
evidence.text:
h1. Purpose
This page describes the required communications for Serving Runtime incidents, including regressions that lead to an emergency rollback.

h1. Who owns comms
* Comms Lead: typically Customer Success oncall (or Support lead after-hours).
* IC approves external messaging for SEV1/SEV2.
* For Dedicated premium SLA tenants, Account Owner must be looped (sales/CS) even during SEV1.

h1. When to post to the public status page
* SEV1: post within 15 minutes of declaration if there is confirmed customer impact in Hosted or multiple Dedicated tenants.
* SEV2: post if impact is user-visible and expected to last > 30 minutes, or if many customers are likely to notice.
* Never post for canary-only SEV3 issues unless instructed by IC.

h1. Required content (status page)
Include:
* What customers observe (symptoms)
* Affected product surface (Hosted API, Dedicated clusters)
* Regions (if known)
* Current mitigation (e.g., paused rollout, rolling back runtime)
* Next update time

h1. Dedicated customer notifications
For Dedicated incidents, in addition to status page (if applicable):
* Email the impacted tenant distribution list and open a support ticket on their behalf (if not already open).
* If the customer has an on-call bridge procedure, ask them to join once we have an ETA or a mitigation plan.

h1. Templates

## Initial status page post (SEV1)
"We are investigating elevated error rates and increased latency affecting the Redwood Inference API in some regions. We have paused the current Serving Runtime rollout and are preparing mitigations. Next update in 30 minutes."

## Update when rollback begins
"We identified a regression in a recent Serving Runtime release and have started an emergency rollback. We are monitoring recovery metrics across regions and will provide an update within 30 minutes."

## Resolved
"The issue has been mitigated and service metrics have returned to normal following a rollback. We will publish a post-incident review."

h1. Approval checklist
Before sending customer-facing comms:
* IC has reviewed the wording
* Do not speculate root cause
* Do not share internal release tags or cluster names unless customer-specific and approved
* If security is suspected, follow the security incident process instead

evidence.title: Emergency change policy (production)
evidence.text:
h1. Policy statement
An *emergency change* is a production change required to mitigate an active or imminent customer-impacting incident. Emergency changes are allowed to bypass standard change windows and review timelines, but must meet the approval and documentation requirements below.

h1. Examples
* Emergency rollback of a Serving Runtime release
* Disabling a faulty feature flag causing elevated 5xx
* Routing traffic away from a degraded region

h1. Minimum required approvals
Emergency changes require at least one of:
* Incident Commander approval (for an active incident), OR
* SRE oncall approval (if no IC assigned yet)

Additional required approvals:
* If the change impacts *Dedicated* customers with premium SLAs: CS oncall or Account Owner must be notified as soon as practical.
* If the change touches authentication, RBAC, audit logging, or encryption: Security oncall must approve.

h1. Documentation requirements
Within 24 hours of the emergency change:
* Create or update the incident record with:
  * what was changed
  * when it was changed
  * who approved
  * verification results
* Link the CI/CD job(s) and dashboards used to validate recovery

h1. Post-change review
* SEV1/SEV2 emergency changes require a postmortem
* During the postmortem, document why standard change management was bypassed and what guardrails will prevent repeat issues

h1. Interaction with releases
If an emergency change is a rollback:
* Pause progressive delivery
* Pin the release tag
* Lock auto-advance until the incident is resolved

h1. References
* Incident SEV process
* Runtime rollback runbook
* Runtime release pipeline rollback procedure

3) Scoring: I'll use Marissa's scorecard and add a short leveling note at the end of my feedback form (explicitly call out cross-team influence and measurable impact).

Olga — please send calendar invite with the meeting link and add the hiring_scorecard.docx to the invite. Alex — see you shortly.

—Aditya
Aditya Rao | Staff Engineer, Serving Runtime
Redwood Inference
"]
