evidence.title: Unified authorizer: core policy evaluator + authorization middleware for API, runtime, and console
evidence.text:
description:
Build RBAC v2 core: a centralized policy evaluation engine plus pluggable authorization middleware to enforce access across the Redwood API (hosted), serving runtime, and Redwood Console. Goals: 1) single consistent policy model and evaluation semantics for API endpoints, runtime token checks, and console UI; 2) native hooks for audit logging and traceability; 3) SSO/SAML and SCIM group-to-role bindings; 4) predictable performance for runtime path (low-latency checks) via fast cache and pre-evaluated bindings; 5) safe migration path from RBAC v1 with feature-flagged rollout and admin controls in Console.

design_decisions:
Policy language: adopt a compact JSON/YAML-based policy schema with CEL expressions for conditions (CEL chosen over Rego for smaller runtime and easier integration with Go services)
Deny-by-default: any unknown resource/action combination results in deny unless an allow policy explicitly matches
Evaluation side-effects: policies must be pure expressions; no side-effects allowed; audit hooks are separate and non-mutating
Sync vs async: API and Console checks are synchronous; runtime token check path uses a hot cache and optional async background refresh for slightly stale bindings
Cache strategy: LRU cache keyed by (principal, resource-type, action) with TTL configurable per deployment; default 30s for runtime, 5s for API gateway
Failure modes: when policy engine is unreachable, fallback policy is configurable per customer: 'fail-closed' for high-security customers, 'fail-open' for low-risk beta customers
SSO mapping: SAML group claims + SCIM provisioning map to role bindings in RBAC v2; mapping rules stored as part of org configuration and evaluated at login and token mint
Admin controls: Console exposes role editor, binding viewer, and audit log filters; destructive role edits require 2-step confirmation and are recorded in audit stream
Migration: RBAC v1 compatibility layer will translate v1 roles into equivalent v2 policies; migration completed per-org with a dry-run mode that logs mismatches
Observability: emit evaluation latency, cache hit/miss, policy compile errors, and per-tenant denied-count metrics to Console dashboards

implementation_plan:
1) Design doc + API contract (Confluence) -> https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/Sec/RBAC+v2+Policy+Engine
2) Core evaluator library in Go (pkg/authorizer) with CEL support; unit tests and fuzz tests
3) API gateway middleware (rest/authorizer) that uses the library and attaches audit events
4) Runtime integration: token-level check hook in serving runtime with optimized in-memory cache and per-GPU node process-local evaluator
5) Console UI: role/binding editor and admin change workflow; integration tests for UI + API
6) Migration tooling: v1->v2 translator and dry-run reporting endpoint
7) End-to-end e2e tests and canary rollout via feature flag 'rbac_v2_enabled'
Implementation PRs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/repo/pull/1234 (core evaluator), https://github.com/redwood-inference/repo/pull/1257 (api middleware), https://github.com/redwood-inference/repo/pull/1289 (console role editor)
Owners: Aisha (design + evaluator), Connor (API gateway + runtime integration), Mei Park (Console UX + integration tests)

rollout_plan:
Phase 0: internal dogfood orgs only, feature flag off for everyone else
Phase 1: canary to 5% of hosted API traffic and <2% runtime traffic on non-critical customers
Phase 2: beta customers opt-in; monitor audit logs and denied-count regressions for 2 weeks
Phase 3: gradual enable by tenant with migration dry-run results cleared and admin sign-off
Fallback plan: quick toggle to RBAC v1 compatibility mode via control-plane command and rollback runbook (ops playbook linked)

acceptance_criteria:
Core evaluator passes unit and fuzz tests; no regressions in benchmark suite (p95 eval latency < 1.2ms cold, <0.3ms hot cache)
API gateway middleware enforces policy for all CRUD endpoints in catalog with audit events emitted to the security audit stream
Runtime token check latency under typical load: additional median latency < 0.5ms with cache enabled
Console role editor allows creating/updating role bindings and logs every admin action to audit logs
Migration translator produces identical allow/deny outcomes for 95% of sampled requests in dry-run across 3 customer orgs
Security review completed and documented; any high severity findings addressed

updates:
2026-02-20: Ticket created. Initial design doc published. Agreed on CEL for policy expressions during architecture sync.
2026-02-26: Prototype evaluator implemented (core/policy) and benchmarked. Cold compile + eval 1.1ms, hot cache 0.28ms. Added initial unit tests.
2026-03-03: Design review with Sec & Infra. Feedback: add stronger telemetry around denied-count spikes and include tenant-level policy version in audit events. Action: Connor to add version header in middleware.
2026-03-06: API middleware PR opened: PR 1257. Incorporated audit event schema: {tenant, principal, resource, action, policy_id, decision, latency_ms}. Linked PR in ticket.
2026-03-09: Security review flagged a risk around SAML group attribute normalization. Mitigation: add canonicalization step and unit tests for unicode/whitespace variants.
2026-03-12: Runtime integration prototype done for dogfood cluster. Observed cache TTL tuning needed (reduced to 15s for hot tenants). Planning canary rollout next sprint.

test_plan:
Unit tests for CEL expressions and type safety
Fuzz tests for policy grammar and invalid inputs
Integration tests: API gateway + Console + evaluator in staging
Performance tests: synthetic load against runtime hook to validate latency SLOs
Migration tests: dry-run compare tool across sample traffic from 3 production tenants

notes:
We will intentionally keep the initial policy schema conservative (no regexes in conditions) to simplify performance guarantees.
Long-term: evaluate storing pre-compiled policy bytecode for microservices to remove compile overhead entirely
Design doc includes examples for common patterns: service-account token read-only bind, dataset-scoped roles, canary deployer role

evidence.title: marketing
evidence.text:
Ethan Wallace: Flagging an external critique we just got on the benchmark. Thread here: https://x.com/latencynerd/status/1800xxxxxxx
Main claim: “Redwood cherry-picked workloads + disabled caching; not fair / not reproducible.”
We should respond once (calm + factual) and link methodology. Need draft language + who posts (Redwood handle vs personal).

Soojin Lee: :eyes: thanks Ethan. Let’s keep it tight and non-defensive. Jonas/Claire can you sanity check what they’re alleging vs what we actually did?

Jonas Weber: Looking now. Their post mixes a few things:
1) They assume we’re using “best-case” concurrency (too high) — we published the concurrency bands + report both p50/p95.
2) They say “caching disabled” — we *disabled cross-request caching* for fairness (no prompt reuse advantages), but batching + KV cache are obviously on as part of serving.
3) “Not reproducible” — we published configs + runner info; full dockerized harness is in the public repo, plus the manifests are in the artifacts.

Claire Dubois: +1. Also, prompt set is not “one cherry-picked prompt.” We used prompt-set v3 production mix (prefill-heavy + decode-heavy blend) and we call that out.
The fair point we can acknowledge: results are workload-dependent. We should invite folks to run their own prompt distribution and share methodology.

Wei Chen: Do we have a single canonical URL we want to point to? Right now landing page has a short methodology summary + the full methodology doc link.
If we want one link, I’d suggest: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/latency-per-dollar#methodology (anchors to the disclaimer + methodology section)

Renee Sullivan: For social reply, I’d propose 2 versions:
- ultra short: “Totally fair to ask. We publish methodology + configs. Note we disable cross-request caching for fairness. Your workload may differ.”
- slightly longer: include bullet list + offer to help replicate.

Ben Carter: Agree: one reply, then stop. We don’t want to spiral.
Also let’s make sure the reply doesn’t over-index on competitor comparisons. The critique is about fairness; keep it about “here’s how we measured.”

Michael Grant: Looping in Legal lens: avoid absolute claims like “most fair,” “definitive,” “proves.”
Safe framing:
- “In our testing…”
- “We designed the methodology to be reproducible and to avoid prompt-reuse advantages…”
- “Workload-dependent; see caveats.”
Don’t accuse the critic of bad faith.

Sofia Mendes: +1. Also avoid saying “we disabled caching” without qualifier — it’ll be misread. Say “cross-request prompt caching was disabled” and explain why.

Soojin Lee: Great. Can we draft a single response we’re all comfortable with and then approve quickly? Noura can post from Redwood account.

Noura El-Khoury: Yep, can post. Need final copy + link(s). If we have a longer explanation, I can keep it as a follow-up reply in-thread.

Rina Kobayashi: Technical specifics we can safely state (all documented):
- Prompt set: v3 production mix (prefill/decode distributions)
- Regions: multiple (NA/EU/APAC where available) with repeated runs
- Warmup + stability gates: rerun if p95 variance > threshold
- Cross-request caching OFF; continuous batching ON
- Metrics: latency/$ + supporting p50/p95, throughput, $/1M tokens

Jonas Weber: One more nuance: “streaming” — we excluded streaming-specific metrics in the main table because apples-to-apples across SDKs/providers is messy; we mention it in caveats. If they bring that up, point to methodology.

Ethan Wallace: Draft response v0 (please edit):
“Totally fair to ask about benchmark methodology. We publish our full ‘how we measured’ (workloads, concurrency, regions, configs) so anyone can reproduce.
For fairness, cross-request prompt caching is disabled (to avoid prompt-reuse advantages), while standard serving optimizations like continuous batching/KV cache are enabled. Results are workload-dependent — see caveats + run details here: <link>”

Wei Chen: Edit suggestion (make it less jargon-y but still precise):
Replace “KV cache” with “inference runtime optimizations (e.g., batching)”?
Though for the technical audience, KV cache is fine.

Markus Klein: From SE angle, we should offer a path: “If you want to run this on your prompts/SLOs, we can share a replication guide.” But on X keep it lightweight.

Soojin Lee: Let’s keep offer minimal: “Happy to compare on a shared workload.” Anything more becomes a sales pitch.

Michael Grant: Proposed tightened copy (legal-safe):
“Good question. We publish our methodology + configs so the results can be reproduced. In our testing, we disable *cross-request prompt caching* to avoid prompt-reuse advantages, and we report p50/p95 + variance checks across repeated runs/regions. Benchmarks are workload-dependent—caveats and details here: <link>”

Sofia Mendes: Looks good. Add “in our testing” early and keep “avoid prompt-reuse advantages” (that’s a clear rationale).

Claire Dubois: Tiny addition: call out prompt set explicitly, since they accuse prompt cherry-picking.
Maybe: “We use a fixed prompt set (v3 production mix) and publish it.”

Jonas Weber: +1. If we mention it, no need to go deep. Just “fixed prompt set” + link.

Ethan Wallace: Updated draft v1:
“Good question. We publish our methodology + configs so results can be reproduced. In our testing we use a fixed prompt set (v3 production mix), disable *cross-request prompt caching* to avoid prompt-reuse advantages, and report p50/p95 with variance checks across repeated runs/regions. Benchmarks are workload-dependent—details + caveats: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/latency-per-dollar#methodology”

Ben Carter: +1 from me. That’s concise and doesn’t escalate.

Noura El-Khoury: Works. I’ll post as Redwood account. Should I also have a second reply ready if they ask “show the configs”?

Rina Kobayashi: If they ask, point to “Artifacts + manifest format” link. Do we have a public repo URL we can share safely?

Wei Chen: Public bench harness link is in the methodology page; there’s also a “Download data” on the interactive table. If they push, reply: “See downloadable run artifacts + schema in the methodology section.”

Soojin Lee: Ok. Noura post the v1 copy. If they respond aggressively, we do not volley. Only one follow-up max that points back to methodology + downloadable artifacts.

Camila Reyes: :thumbsup: This is the tone we want. After posting, drop the link in #announcements if it starts getting traction so CS/Sales aren’t surprised.

Noura El-Khoury: Posted from @RedwoodInference with the v1 copy + methodology link. Will monitor for 30–60m.

Ethan Wallace: Thanks all. I’ll also update the internal FAQ doc later today with this exact language as “canonical response to fairness critique” so Support can reuse.

Jonas Weber: If we get a follow-up asking about caching specifically, we can reuse this line:
“Cross-request prompt caching is off for fairness; the runtime still uses standard inference optimizations (continuous batching, KV cache) that are part of normal serving.”

Soojin Lee: Perfect. Closing loop here unless anything changes.

evidence.title: Predictive Batching & Cost Optimizer PRD
evidence.text:
Overview:

This PRD describes Predictive Batching & Cost Optimizer (PBCO), a product initiative in Redwood Optimize that dynamically chooses batching strategies, model variants, and quantization profiles to minimize per-token cost while meeting customer latency SLOs. PBCO targets mid-to-large production customers that run latency-sensitive generation workloads and want automatic cost reductions without manual tuning.

Goals:
- Reduce average token cost for eligible workloads by 25% (median) within 90 days of rollout for enrolled tenants.
- Maintain 95th percentile tail latency within configured SLOs (per-tenant).
- Provide transparent telemetry and an "explain" UI that shows why batching decisions were made for a request.
- Support hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments with feature parity for policy controls.

Non-goals:
- Model training or fine-tuning optimizations (out of scope).
- Replacing customer-controlled batching at the SDK-level; PBCO operates in the serving/control plane and can be disabled.

User Journeys:
1) Self-serve (small engineering team):
   - Enable "Cost Optimizer" in the Console toggles (default off).
   - Provide workload profile (interactive chat, background job, max_latency_ms).
   - System runs a 48-hour dry-run and reports estimated savings and risk.
   - User chooses roll-forward or custom policy.

2) Enterprise (platform/ops):
   - Create tenant policy: hard SLO 300ms p95, max cost uplift 10% allowed, approved model families.
   - Schedule canary on subset of routes (5% traffic) for 7 days.
   - Platform owner reviews explain logs and approves global rollout.

Success metrics (KPIs):
- Cost reduction: median per-token cost delta for participating traffic (target -25%).
- Stability: p95 latency delta vs SLO (target <= 0% breach rate increase).
- Accuracy/Quality regressions: percentage of eval prompt-sets with regression alerts (target < 1%).
- Adoption: % of enterprise customers enabling PBCO within 3 months of GA (>20%).

Architecture and components (high level):
- Predictor Service: time-series model that predicts request arrival patterns per route/tenant (windowed).
- Decision Engine: applies tenant policies, predicted queueing latency, and kernel-level perf profiles to choose: batch size, batching delay, model variant (full/quantized/LLM-smaller), and cache reuse policy.
- Runtime Hooks: lightweight runtime integration points that apply selected configuration per-request (batch boundary signals, quantization switch, KV cache hints).
- Telemetry & Explain Store: stores decision inputs and outputs for each request to power the explain UI and offline analysis.
- Dry-run Simulator: runs decisions in a sandbox against live traffic to estimate savings and quality impact without affecting production.

API surface and configuration (examples):
1) Tenant policy resource (JSON example shown as text):

{
  "policy_id": "string",
  "routes": ["/chat/*", "/summarize/*"],
  "p95_latency_ms": 300,
  "allowed_models": ["redwood-large-v2", "redwood-medium-q4"],
  "max_allowed_quality_delta_pct": 1.0,
  "batching_presets": ["aggressive","balanced","conservative"],
  "dry_run": true
}

2) Runtime knob CLI (examples):
- rcli optimize enable --tenant my-tenant --policy-id policy-2026-11
- rcli optimize simulate --policy policy-2026-11 --window 48h --output csv

Configuration table (human-readable):
| config_key | type | default | notes |
|---------------------------|--------|---------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| p95_latency_ms            | int    | 200     | Target 95th percentile tail latency for route/tenant in milliseconds |
| allowed_models            | list   | [*]     | Model family whitelist; * means any compatible variant permitted      |
| batching_preset           | enum   | balanced| aggressive=high savings, conservative=low risk                     |
| quality_delta_threshold   | float  | 1.0     | % change in eval metric tolerated before rollback                   |

Rollout plan and milestones:
- Phase 0 — Research & Benchmarks (complete): predictive model MAPE <= 12% on representative routes; batcher microbenchmarks show 15–40% perf delta across kernel sets.
- Phase 1 — Internal dry-run (2 months): enable for 100% internal traffic via simulator, run scenario tests, validate explain artifacts.
- Phase 2 — Select-customer canaries (3 months):
  1) Invite five high-usage customers (diverse workload profiles).
  2) Run sequential canaries per customer (traffic ramp 1% -> 5% -> 20%).
  3) Collect quality evals and uptime/latency telemetry.
- Phase 3 — Gradual GA (4 weeks): opt-in GA for all hosted customers with Console toggle and API flag.
- Phase 4 — Dedicated/Private enablement (post-GA): provide operator-run installers and KMS/HSM guidance for sensitive environments.

Pricing & packaging impact:
- The Optimizer will be a paid add-on with a two-part model: (1) a fixed monthly subscription tier (Optimize Standard / Optimize Enterprise) and (2) a revenue share on measured gross savings above a baseline for the first 90 days.
- Suggested public SKUs: optimize.standard, optimize.enterprise. Standard includes up to 10 routes, enterprise includes SLA and audit logging.
- Billing example: tenant A baseline per-token spend $12000/month. After optimizer, measured spend $9000/month (gross savings $3000). Revenue share 15% for first 90 days -> invoice add-on $450 + monthly subscription.
- Manual override: billing only applies for tenants that explicitly opt in to savings-share; dry-run insights are free.

Quality and acceptance tests (must pass for GA):
1) Functional: decision engine returns legal config combos for 100% of sampled requests.
2) Perf: system achieves at least 10% cost reduction in the simulator for 75% of sample routes.
3) Latency safety: no SLO breach introduced in 99.9% of simulator cases.
4) Eval-based regressions: for each customer prompt-set, regressions must be below configured quality_delta_threshold.
5) Observability: explain logs available for 100% of canary traffic; Console shows per-route breakdown.

Monitoring, Telemetry and Alerts:
- Metrics to emit: optimizer.decisions.count, optimizer.savings.per_tenant, optimizer.quality_regressions.count, optimizer.p95_latency_impact.
- SLOs for the product itself: optimizer decision latency <50ms 99th percentile.
- Alert rules (example):
  - Severity P1: tenant p95 latency increase > 10% for 5m after a policy change -> page SRE and product.
  - Severity P2: quality regression alert rate > 1% across canary prompts -> notify owners and pause optimizer for affected routes.

Operational runbook (short):
1) When an oncall page hits for latency spikes, run: rcli optimize inspect --tenant <id> --since 10m
2) To roll back policy: rcli optimize disable --tenant <id> --policy <id>
3) To pause global optimizer: console -> Admin -> Optimize -> Global Pause (requires two-person approval).

Open risks & mitigations:
- Risk: Undetected quality regressions in niche prompts -> Mitigation: require customer-provided prompt-sets for canary, enforce conservative default for unseen routes.
- Risk: Interaction with Dedicated capacity autoscaler -> Mitigation: decision engine queries capacity metadata and respects reserved pool limits.

evidence.title: GPU BIOS & Firmware Orchestration — IaC Spec and Runbook
evidence.text:
OVERVIEW:

This page defines the specification, Terraform/IaC contracts, CI/CD pipeline, monitoring, and on-call runbook for coordinated BIOS and firmware updates on Redwood GPU fleet nodes. BIOS and base firmware updates are high-risk operations that can affect node bootability, driver compatibility, and inference SLOs; this doc codifies a safe, repeatable process tied to IaC metadata so updates are auditable, reversible, and can be phased across accounts/regions.

Audience and scope:
- Primary: eng-infra, eng-sre, eng-serving-runtime.
- Scope: Fleet-owned GPU hosts (bare-metal and cloud VM accelerators) under Redwood management; NOT customer-managed Private nodes.
- Excludes OS kernel/security patching workflows (covered in infra-image-rotation).

Goals and design principles:
- Safety-first: every update must provide an automated rollback path and pre-flight validation.
- Declarative metadata: firmware versions and desired BIOS configurations are expressed via Terraform variables and tag-based selectors.
- Minimal blast radius: phased canaries by topology (AZ, rack, instance-family).
- Observability: telemetry and automated health checks detect boot regressions within 10 minutes of update.
- Traceability: updates are recorded with audit metadata (operator, changelist, checksum).

Key concepts and terminology:
- Update Bundle: signed archive containing firmware binaries, vendor tooling, and a manifest (sha256 checksums + supported kernel/driver matrix).
- Node Selector: tag expression used by the provisioner to choose nodes (e.g., account:gpu-prod && instance-profile:a100-80g && rack:us-west-2a-row3).
- Drift Tag: fleet tag applied to nodes that have diverged from desired firmware (redwood:firmware_state=drift).
- Safe Mode Boot: a temporary boot configuration that prevents multi-GPU drivers from initializing; used for rollback validation when supported.

IaC / Terraform contract (module summary):
- Module name: redwood_gpu_firmware_operator
- Purpose: register an Update Bundle, define target selectors, and create a controlled run record for the orchestration pipeline.
- High-level variables (table):
| variable | type | description | example |
|----------|------|-------------|---------|
| name | string | human id for the update | "nv-bios-2026q1-a100" |
| bundle_s3_uri | string | signed bundle archive location | "s3://redwood-firmware/nv/2026q1.tar.gz" |
| checksum | string | sha256 of bundle | "abcdef..." |
| node_selector | string | terraform tag expression (see examples) | "account == 'gpu-prod' && family == 'a100-80g'" |
| canary_fraction | string | fractional canary (0.0 - 1.0) | "0.02" |
| maintenance_window | string | UTC cron window for apply | "Mon-Fri 01:00-04:00" |
| preflight_playbook_id | string | id of validation job (CI) | "firmware-preflight-42" |
| owner | string | primary owner/team | "eng-infra" |

- Outputs (module):
  - run_id: unique orchestration run id (string)
  - bundle_manifest: artifact metadata reference
  - planned_targets: list of node ids (as CSV)

Terraform usage example:
```hcl
module "nv_bios_q1" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo.redwood/infra/modules//gpu_firmware_operator"
  name = "nv-bios-2026q1-a100"
  bundle_s3_uri = "s3://redwood-firmware/nv/2026q1-a100.tar.gz"
  checksum = "sha256:..."
  node_selector = "account == 'gpu-prod' && family == 'a100-80g' && region == 'us-west-2'"
  canary_fraction = "0.01"
  maintenance_window = "Tue 02:00-05:00 UTC"
  preflight_playbook_id = "firmware-preflight-42"
  owner = "eng-infra"
}
```

Preflight validation (CI job):
- The preflight CI job validates the bundle against the supported kernel/driver matrix and then runs a signed emulation harness that verifies the vendor flashing tool returns green for a synthetic device.
- Commands (example):
  - vendor-tool verify --bundle s3://... --manifest manifest.json
  - ./validate-driver-compatibility.sh --bundle manifest.json --kernel 6.5.4 --driver 545.92
- Preflight must produce a signed attestation object uploaded to the bundle S3 path; Terraform module references that attestation before enabling the run.

Orchestration flow (high-level):
1. Terraform registers Update Bundle via module (creates Run record, planned_targets output).
2. Operator pipeline validates attestation and locks target nodes into pre-update state (sets redwood:firmware_lock=true).
3. Canary phase: the worker selects N nodes based on canary_fraction and topology spread.
4. Apply bundle on canaries with vendor tooling via ephemeral GPU maintenance container; run boot checks and runtime smoke tests.
5. Monitor for 30 minutes (configurable) for metrics regressions; if green, promote rollout to next wave.
6. Roll waves until all planned_targets are patched or until failure triggers rollback.

Canary policy and topology spread:
- Default canary fraction: 1% of matching nodes, min 2 nodes, max 10 nodes per wave.
- Spread constraints: prefer different racks and AZs, prefer low load tenants (evict ephemeral eval before selecting).
- Wave cadence: default 60–90 minutes between waves (observability dependent).

Monitoring & SLOs to watch (thresholds):
- Node boot success rate: target 99.95%; alert if < 99% across canaries within 15 minutes.
- GPU daemon readiness (driver + nvrm): must reach Ready state within 10 minutes of reboot; alert if >10% of canaries fail.
- Inference latency p50/p95 for impacted model routes: p95 degradation > 30% triggers rollback evaluation.
- Kernel oops or dmesg errors with NV vendor strings: page to oncall and pause rollout.
- Node-level panic or non-responsive consoles: immediate abort and automatic rollback for other waves.

Automated rollback criteria (examples):
- Any node in canary reports boot failure or fails runtime smoke tests.
- Aggregate p95 latency increase for any production model > 50% over baseline during the observation window.
- More than 3% of canaries emit driver requeue/fatal errors.
- Manual abort by release owner or SRE on-call.

Rollback strategy:
- If a canary fails, the orchestrator automatically attempts a rollback on that node using the previous bundle (bundle metadata stored in run history).
- If a failure pattern indicates a systemic issue, orchestrator aborts all pending waves and schedules rollback jobs across all updated nodes.
- Rollback steps: reflash previous firmware image -> boot -> run smoke tests -> clear drift tags -> update run record.

On-call runbook (condensed):
1. Page received: "firmware-orchestrator: canary-failure" with run_id.
2. Open run dashboard: check planned_targets, completed_waves, failed_nodes.
3. Check boot logs: `journalctl -u systemd -b -o cat` and vendor flash logs at `/var/log/firmware-flash.log` (persisted to central s3).
4. If node shows boot failure: attach serial console (cloud-systems) or repro via iDRAC/IPMI. Attempt remote power-cycle.
5. If driver initialization fails: capture dmesg and NVIDIA vendor logs, escalate to runtime owners.
6. If rollback is necessary: hit the orchestrator rollback API with run_id and reason. Follow post-rollback verification checklist: run smoke tests, confirm driver ready, clear firmware_lock tag.
7. Post-incident: update the run record with root cause and tag related jira/card.

Operational considerations and checklist:
- Pre-maintenance checklist (to be completed before registration):
  - Confirm backup images exist for the previous firmware and are validated.
  - Confirm maintenance window scheduled and owner approved.
  - Notify Product/SRE stakeholders and open a transient incident docket.
  - Confirm ephemeral workloads evacuated from targeted nodes.
- During update checklist:
  - Ensure telemetry export (boot traces, flash logs) is enabled and uploaded in real-time.
  - Verify automated smoke tests include at least: kernel module load, CUDA basic vector ops, small inference round-trip.
- Post-update checklist:
  - Reconcile run record with Terraform state and attach attestation.
  - Check for drift tags and run remediation for any nodes not successfully updated.

Roles and ownership:
- Release owner: eng-infra release manager (primary contact for go/no-go)
- On-call escalation: eng-sre primary pager, eng-serving-runtime secondary
- IaC module maintainers: infra-plat team (module and variable contracts)
- Firmware validation: research/applied-ml for model-run smoke tests and perf baselines

Security and compliance notes:
- All bundles must be signed with the vendor key and verified on ingestion; unsigned bundles are rejected.
- Access to S3 firmware artifacts is limited to the operator role; key usage is audited.
- For customer-affecting Private deployments, follow Private deployment firmware policy and require CISO approval for vendor-signed binaries.

Audit and post-mortem artifacts:
- Orchestrator run record contains: run_id, bundle checksum, operator, start/end timestamps, wave-by-wave results, telemetry snapshots (p95 latency, node boot logs).
- Records are exported to the central audit-index (ELK) and attached to the CI/CD release tag.

Appendix: Useful commands and examples:
- List planned targets (from module output): `redwoodctl runs describe --run-id $RUN_ID --fields planned_targets`
- Force a rollback via API: `redwoodctl runs rollback $RUN_ID --reason "canary boot fails" --auto-force`
- Sample manifest snippet (manifest.json in bundle):
  {
    "bundle_version": "2026-01-10",
    "supported_kernels": ["6.4.0", "6.5.4"],
    "images": ["bios.bin", "bmc_fw.bin"],
    "checksums": {"bios.bin": "sha256:...", "bmc_fw.bin": "sha256:..."}
  }

Related pages and references:
- infra-image-rotation-and-cve-response-runbook (image rotation)
- cuda-driver-provenance-and-rolling-upgrade-playbook (driver upgrades)
- oncall-gpu-egress-surge-mitigation-and-traffic-shaping-runbook (oncall links)

Change log:
- 2025-09-16: Initial draft by Priya Nair.
- 2025-12-03: Added Terraform contract and preflight attestation requirement (reviewed by Ethan Park).
- 2026-01-12: Finalized monitoring thresholds and rollback criteria (published).

Contact: priya.nair@redwood.ai for questions or to schedule a rollout test.

evidence.title: eng-infra
evidence.text:
Alex: Heads up — after the 02:00 UTC BMC firmware roll (vendor image 2.4.1 -> 2.5.0) ~12 nodes in gpunode-dedicated-usw1 are failing to PXE. Symptoms: POST stops at 'No bootable device' when Secure Boot is enabled.

Maria: Oof. Which nodes? error logs?

Alex: node ids: gpu-usw1-042..053 (12 total). Quick ipmi dump: 
```
ipmitool -H gpu-usw1-042 -U admin mc info
Device ID : 32
Firmware Revision : 2.5.0
Manufacturer ID : 12345
Product ID : 678
```
Boot looks sane when SecureBoot=false. When enabled, firmware rejects our signed PXE shim.

Dinesh: Are these Dedicated pool machines or Private?

Alex: Dedicated pool (reserved commit). Impacting scheduled training queues and a handful of low-priority infra jobs. Draining now.

Priya: Did the roll intentionally flip Secure Boot? Vendor notes mention a default toggle in 2.5.0 for some SKUs. Can we patch that flag remotely?

Alex: Trying Redfish PATCH now: 
```
curl -k -u admin:REDACTED https://10.4.22.42/redfish/v1/Systems/1/Bios -X PATCH -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"SecureBoot":false}'
```
One node accepted it and rebooted to PXE. But console for others shows "Secure Boot policy mismatch".

SRE-Bot: Scheduled maintenance window closed automatically at 03:00 UTC. Host-level changes after window require manual ack :warning: 

Ryan: We should treat this like a severity-2 until capacity recovers. What % of GPU capacity lost?

Alex: Rough calc: 12 nodes = ~84 A100 GPUs (~8% of west-us pool). Queues ramping.

Dinesh: Short term mitigation: 1) Drain affected nodes (Alex doing), 2) Route new jobs to other regions / burst to cloud spot, 3) Start rollback plan to 2.4.1 for nodes that won't accept remote SecureBoot toggle.

Priya: I can coordinate rollback for 6 nodes (we have physical console access via OOB team). Need oncall windows for the rest.

Maria: Any chance of re-signing the PXE shim with vendor key? That is longer path.

Alex: Vendor engineering said 2.5.0 introduced stricter signature checks; their recommended fixes: a) disable SecureBoot remotely, b) roll BMC back to 2.4.1, or c) update shim signed by vendor key. They pushed an internal KB: https://redwood.share/internal/kb/bmc-2.5-secureboot-change (link)

Dinesh: Cost question — if we burst to cloud to cover training windows, estimate?

Ryan: If we shift 84 A100-equivalent GPU-hrs/day to cloud on demand it's ~ $1.8k/day. If we use spot probably half but higher risk. Need finance signoff for >48hr.

Alex: Action items: 
- Alex: finish cordon/drain for the 12 nodes and move jobs (in progress)
- Priya: coordinate physical rollback for 6 with OOB team (assigned)
- Dinesh: open SEV with vendor, escalate to account team (assigned)
- Maria: update runbook with Redfish snippet + rollback steps: https://redwood.share/runbooks/bmc-firmware (updating)

Priya: Runbook snippet I'm adding: 
```
# disable secure boot via Redfish
PATCH /redfish/v1/Systems/1/Bios
{ "SecureBoot": false }
# verify
GET /redfish/v1/Systems/1
```
Note: some vendors require /Managers/1/BIOS path.

Alex: Quick `kubectl` commands used for drain: 
```
kubectl cordon gpu-usw1-042
kubectl drain gpu-usw1-042 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
```
Jobs moved, cluster autoscaler kicked in for remaining capacity.

SRE-Bot: Auto-alert: queue 'training-prod' slipped SLA 3x in last 15m. Paging: @oncall-sre.

Dinesh: Vendor response ETA 2 hours, said they are reproducing in lab. Requested serial logs and BMC dumps.

Ryan: If vendor ETA slips past 4 hours, submit finance request for cloud burst. Otherwise keep holding.

Alex: Update: Rolled back BMC to 2.4.1 on 10/12 nodes via OOB console 04:36 UTC — those nodes came back and rejoined. Two nodes require rack-level presence (NIC not responding to Redfish). Opening a parts ticket. Capacity back to ~98%.

Priya: Will file hardware ticket for the two on-site nodes and schedule tech visit tomorrow PST.

Maria: Great job moving fast. Please add final postmortem notes to incidents/ after we finish vendor RCA.

Alex: Will do. Adding timeline + commands to runbook now. :white_check_mark:

evidence.title: Microphone fails to enumerate after BIOS flash + Secure Boot toggle during depot repair
evidence.text:
description:
Issue summary: After a standard depot BIOS flash followed by toggling Secure Boot to re-enable legacy imaging paths, attached device microphones (internal array) no longer enumerate in Windows. Observed on small subset of fleet following recent vendor BIOS (v1.18.4) rollout to depot units.

Impact: Affected users see "No audio input device installed" in Settings and Device Manager; internal microphone missing from audio input list. External USB microphones still function. This blocks users from joining voice calls and impacts QA signoff for a subset of refurbished laptops. Approximately 7 confirmed units to date, all processed through the same depot workflow.

Environment: Depot repair/flash workflow, corp provisioning image (Win11-23H2-corp), Secure Boot toggled from Enabled -> Disabled -> Enabled during repair validation; BIOS version 1.18.4 on affected units.

Observed behavior: After reboot, Windows audio subsystem loads but Microphone Array device does not appear in Device Manager; no driver nodes for the audio DSP. Windows Event Log shows Service Control Manager entries for audioendpointbuilder failing to start dependent driver with Code 7000. Kernel logs show ACPI _DSM calls returning different hardware IDs after Secure Boot toggle.

Expected behavior: Internal microphone enumerates and appropriate audio codec driver (vendor) is present under Sound, video and game controllers and Audio inputs and outputs.

Notes: This ticket is an internal support/depot-repair workflow issue; not customer-facing. Triage requested to determine whether the BIOS change altered firmware visibility or audio codec microcontroller (DSP) firmware got re-flashed/disabled when Secure Boot state changed.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Take affected model (Lenovo X1 Gen10 / Dell 7440) with BIOS v1.18.4.
2) Run depot BIOS flash script (vendor recommended image).
3) During imaging validate, toggle Secure Boot: Enabled -> Disabled -> Enabled (this is part of depot validation for legacy imaging fallback).
4) Boot into WinPE, apply corp image and driver pack, complete OOBE and restart.
5) Log in and open Settings > System > Sound and Device Manager > Audio inputs and outputs.
6) Observe missing internal microphone; external USB mic enumerates.
7) Collect Windows Event Logs (System/Application) and run 'pnputil /enum-devices' and 'driverquery /v'.

logs:
System event: Service Control Manager 7000 - The AudioEndpointBuilder service failed to start due to the following error: The driver failed to load.
Kernel: ACPI: _DSM returned HWID mismatch for HDAUDIO device after Secure Boot toggle (trace id: acpi-evt-20260310-01).
Device manager output: No 'Microphone Array' under 'Audio inputs and outputs'.
Driver pack installer log: vendor-audio-driver.inf skipped: signature validation failed (policy: secureboot-recheck).

investigation_notes:
03/10 Aisha: Initial triage at depot - reproduced on 2/7 units processed this morning. Verified BIOS version and image steps; Secure Boot toggled per depot checklist.
03/11 Ethan: Collected Event Logs and performed driver pack install manually. Observed INF skipped due to signature validation when Secure Boot state set to Enabled at end of workflow. When Secure Boot is left Disabled, driver installs and microphone appears—indicates SB interplay with vendor driver signing or firmware validation.
03/11 Hardware Tech (Maya): Dumped audio DSP firmware via vendor tool on affected unit; firmware blob present but manifest signature mismatch reported after BIOS flash + SB toggle sequence. Vendor firmware component appears intact but bootloader rejects it when SB re-enabled without vendor key/manifest present.
03/12 Eng (Ravi): Compared BIOS release notes; 1.18.4 adds an 'audio codec lockdown' feature that enforces signature verification of codec firmware if Secure Boot is Enabled. Our depot workflow toggles SB, which causes the pre-boot manifest to be rewritten by vendor tool under Disabled state; re-enabling SB makes the manifest fail signature checks.

comments:
Aisha Malik (2026-03-10): Created ticket after depot tech reported 2 units. Assigned to Ethan for deep-dive.
Ethan Park (2026-03-11): Reproduced locally in lab. Workaround: keep Secure Boot Disabled until vendor-signed driver/manifest installed. Need to avoid leaving SB toggled in depot workflow.
Maya Chen - Depot Tech (2026-03-11): Confirmed vendor tool can reflash codec firmware if bootloader unlocked; process takes ~6 minutes per unit. Requires vendor-provided signed manifest to pass SB validation.
Ravi Patel - Firmware (2026-03-12): Reached out to vendor support thread; vendor acknowledged change and provided internal ticket RDL-4621. Waiting on signed manifest and updated driver pack.

resolution_notes:
Mitigation (short-term): Depot procedure updated to NOT re-enable Secure Boot until after vendor-signed driver pack and codec manifest are installed. Depot checklist version bumped to 2026-03-12_v2. Deployed a temporary step in SCCM task sequence to force-install vendor driver when SB is Disabled.
Patch plan (medium-term): Vendor to deliver signed codec manifest + updated driver pack. Eng to validate on staging images and then push driver pack to driver-packs repo (PR referenced).
Follow-ups: 1) Add a pre-imaging validation that detects BIOS 1.18.4 and flags units for 'codec manifest restore' step. 2) Add automation to depot telemetry to capture microphone enumeration status post-imaging. 3) Post-mortem with vendor and update runbook (confluence page) to include this signature interplay.

evidence.title: eng-infra
evidence.text:
Lee: FYI — during tonight's eu-west firmware push one of our canary racks (rack-r13) had a nasty surprise. 4 nodes failed to boot after BIOS+BMC updates, two of them have no OOB console responses. Secure boot appears to have been toggled on by the new BIOS on a subset, blocking Ubuntu shim.

Maria: ack. Which models and how many GPUs impacted?

Lee: Dell R750xa, 8 nodes in the canary group; 4 failed to come back. That's 32x A100s offline logically (4 nodes * 8 gpus). Losing that capacity is already impacting Dedicated eu-west queues; we had to burst to on-demand which is ~+$600/day in extra cost. :grimacing:

Dan: grabbing ipmi/console logs now. On two nodes ipmitool can't even open a session (connection timed out). On the others we see secure boot errors in the syslog during kernel handoff.

Lee: sample ipmitool output from one of the partially responsive nodes:

```
# ipmitool -I lanplus -H 10.3.21.45 -U ADMIN -P **** mc info
Device ID               : 32
Device Revision         : 1
Firmware Revision       : 2.12
IPMI Version            : 2.0
Manufacturer ID         : 47488
Manufacturer Name       : Dell Inc.
Product ID              : 1
Aux Firmware Rev Info   : 0x0
```

Dan: and the BMC log tail shows repeated watchdog resets and a failed NVMe passthrough during init: 

```
[2026-05-04T02:12:11Z] BMC: watchdog reset
[2026-05-04T02:12:12Z] BMC: nvme-passthru init failed: rc=-5
[2026-05-04T02:12:12Z] BIOS: secure boot enabled by default
[2026-05-04T02:12:12Z] OS: shim verification failed
```

Sophie: sounds like the new BIOS defaults to enabling secure boot and some images don't have the signed shim. Did the vendor note any secure-boot default flip in the release notes?

Arjun: I skimmed their CU (FW release notes) — they mention "secure boot policy alignment" but not explicit defaults. We should escalate to Dell to confirm.

Lee: I've paused the rollout for the rest of eu-west. Can we roll back the BMC image on the 4 failed nodes to previous stable and flip secure boot off as a quick patch?

Maria: rolling back BMC remotely requires a responsive BMC. For the two with no OOB we might need on-site power-cycle or iDRAC rescue USB. I've opened a ticket with onsite techs to physically power-cycle and plug in a BMC console dongle.

OncallBot: Incident created: INC-2026-0423 — eu-west firmware canary failures. Priority: P2. Affected capacity: ~32 GPUs. Assigned: eng-infra.

Dan: For the two nodes where bmc responds we can try racadm to set SecureBoot off and then reboot:

```
racadm --nocertwarn setbiosupp SecureBootEnable 0
racadm serveraction powercycle
```

Sophie: If racadm doesn't work we'll try ipmitool raw to flip UEFI vars, but that's brittle. Also want to avoid mass disabling secure boot across prod without vendor sign-off.

Lee: Agreed. Action plan: 
- rollback BMC on the 2 responsive nodes and set SecureBoot=0 (Dan/Maria)
- onsite techs to power-cycle + serial console capture for the 2 unresponsive nodes (Maria)
- Dell support engaged to validate the firmware defaults and provide hotpatch or explicit rollback procedure (Lee -> DellSupport)
- keep rollout paused (Lee)

Arjun: I'll run a quick capacity reconciliation and estimate impact to SLAs and costs. If we need to run more on-demand for the next 48 hrs it's ~ $1.2k extra. Putting note in the cost tracker.

DellSupport: Thanks, we've pulled the release notes and reproduced a similar symptom in lab. Looks like BMC v2.12 + BIOS 1.45 combo may set a Secure Boot flag on certain SKUs. We're escalating to engineering, ETA for hotfix: 8-12 hrs. For immediate workaround use racadm to flip SecureBoot and boot, or reflash BIOS to 1.44 image.

Maria: racadm flip worked on node r13n04. Node came back, kubelet re-joined, GPU counts restored for that pod. Two nodes still offline pending onsite.

Lee: good. Please document exact commands and file them under eng-infra runbooks. Also let's add a preflight check for SecureBoot bits in the firmware rollout playbook so we don't hit this again.

Dan: noted, I'll add a `fw_preflight.sh` step that runs `dmidecode` and `sbctl` checks after BIOS stage and before BMC finalize.

Sophie: Can we also add a cost alert when Dedicated eu-west spare falls below 10%? We had to burst earlier than expected.

Arjun: putting that in monitoring board now.

Lee: thanks all. We'll reconvene in 2 hrs or sooner if Dell provides a hotfix. :thumbsup:

evidence.title: eng-infra
evidence.text:
sasha: FYI — after the BIOS bump (datacenter-bios-2026-02-17) on rack-12, six GPU nodes' BMCs are dropping into a secure-boot locked state and refusing PXE. Affected: rw-gpu-1201..1206. :warning:
jun: when did the rollout start and which orchestration job?
sasha: started 02:10 UTC via job `fw-rollout-2`. changed BMC and system BIOS at the same time.
maria: monitoring shows OOB heartbeats flapped then came back but no BMC shell/SSH. I see redfish 423 on a couple nodes.
alex: tried curl against rw-gpu-1201 redfish, retrieving SecureBoot endpoint returns status LOCKED and action denied.
sasha: example quick check (no creds here):
```bash
# sample Redfish check (do not paste creds in channel)
curl -k -u admin:REDACTED https://10.0.5.201/redfish/v1/Systems/1/BIOS/SecureBoot -X GET
```
jun: please don't share creds in chat. Steps we can try: ipmitool mc reset, try Redfish Manager->SecureBoot toggle, or revert BMC image. ipmitool example: `ipmitool -I lanplus -H 10.0.5.201 -U admin mc reset cold`.
maria: note: GPUs (H100s here) require BIOS microcode match. If we start cycling nodes without the GPU microcode update, we risk NVLink failures and kernel panics on resume. Need a careful plan.
alex: my read: BMC accepted the new firmware but secure boot keystore wasn't populated correctly during the migration. So the system flips to locked mode until keys are present; that blocks PXE/remote boot.
sasha: ops-bot, open incident and tag oncall please. we need approval for out-of-band key injection.
ops-bot: Incident created: INC-20260317-3. Priority: P2. Owner: eng-infra.
jun: cost/impact note: each node counts toward Dedicated reserved capacity. If these 6 nodes stay down for 3 hours that's ~ $120/hr per node — quick math says this is not cheap. Need to minimize time.
maria: proposed immediate plan:
1) pause the rollout globally
2) move affected nodes to maintenance pool (no traffic)
3) attempt key injection/revert to previous BMC on one node as test
4) if successful, roll rest in small batches with validation hooks
5) update orchestration to include keysync step before toggling secure boot
Can we get a maintenance window at 04:00 UTC?
jun: I'll take the first node (rw-gpu-1201) for rollback and key injection test. tagging oncall.
alex: quick manual commands for reference (ops-only):
```bash
# ipmitool reset BMC
ipmitool -I lanplus -H 10.0.5.201 -U admin -P <redacted> mc reset cold
# sample racadm update (Dell iDRAC) - adjust per vendor
racadm fwupdate -g -u /tmp/bmc_fw.bin
# Redfish example to POST secure keys (vendor-specific) - placeholder

evidence.title: Smart Contract Audit Assistant — POC scoping and pricing (draft)
evidence.text:
Context and goal:

This document is a draft scoping and pricing proposal for a 6‑week POC to evaluate Redwood Inference’s Smart Contract Audit Assistant (SCAA) for a mid‑market blockchain security firm. The customer has asked for an assistive tool that speeds manual audits by surfacing likely vulnerability sites, generating succinct human‑readable findings, and producing reproducible test snippets. The POC will validate accuracy, latency on private deployments, data isolation, and integration into the customer’s triage workflow.

High level objectives (success criteria):
- Reduce average time to triage a flagged contract from initial scan to first actionable finding by >= 40% (measured across sampled audit tasks).
- Achieve a precision >= 78% and recall >= 65% against the customer’s curated vulnerability test set (150 labelled examples).
- Demonstrate private deployment (VPC) with customer‑managed keys and audit logging that meets their baseline compliance checklist.
- Integrate with the customer’s existing Jira‑style tracker so model output can be turned into reproducible issues.

Scope of work (6 weeks POC):
1) Kickoff & data collection (Week 0–1)
   - 90m kickoff with engineering + security stakeholders to align goals and define measurement plan.
   - Customer provides representative sample corpus (up to 1,000 contracts, mix of Solidity/Vyper), labelling guidelines, and example triage tickets.
   - Agree on redaction policy and any sensitive data handling constraints.

2) Model selection & prompt engineering (Week 1–2)
   - Evaluate 2–3 open model backbones (quantized variants) on a small held‑out subset for vulnerability classification and finding summarization.
   - Create prompt templates and structured output schema (severity, vulnerability type, vuln location snippet, suggested reproduction steps, confidence).

3) Private deployment & integration (Week 2–4)
   - Provision Redwood Private VPC environment (customer network peering) or air‑gapped package as required.
   - Integrate customer KMS for key encryptions, enable audit logs, and configure role‑based access.
   - Implement a connector that converts model outputs into the customer’s ticketing format (sample Jira attachments/webhook).

4) Evaluation & tuning (Week 4–5)
   - Run batch evaluation against the labelled test set and compute precision/recall, per‑vulnerability-type breakdown, latency P95/P99 for end‑to‑end inference (including pre/post processing).
   - Tune batching, KV caching, and prompt variants to meet latency/SLO targets (aim for < 1.2s per inference for a 200‑line contract snippet in interactive flows).

5) Workshop & handoff (Week 5–6)
   - 2‑hour review workshop: present metrics, sample outputs, false positives/negatives, operational runbook for model updates, and recommended rollout path.
   - Deliverables: evaluation notebook, sample connector code, deployment runbook, and a one‑page executive summary.

Deliverables (explicit):
- POC Deployment: fully functional SCAA instance in customer VPC or on‑prem trial bundle.
- Evaluation Report: quantitative metrics, error analysis, prompt recipes, and suggested model/quantization profiles.
- Integration Artifacts: connector for ticket creation, example CI snippets for continuous test generation, and sample unit tests.
- Operational Docs: runbook for scaling, cost profiling, access control matrix, and incident playbook.
- Executive One‑Pager summarizing ROI and recommended next steps.

Assumptions (important):
- Customer provides representative corpus and at least 150 labelled examples for initial evaluation within 7 business days after kickoff.
- Networking: customer will enable peering/VPN with Redwood Private or accept the on‑prem deployment appliance image.
- No formal SOC2 or FedRAMP audit is included in the POC. If required, add a separate compliance engagement.
- Performance numbers assume 1–2 concurrent interactive users and a reserved GPU for the trial; multi‑tenant load testing is out of scope for the POC.

Pricing (POC fixed fee with optional add‑ons):
- Base POC (6 weeks): $75,000 fixed. Includes engineering time (prototype integration, prompt engineering, evaluation), private trial infra (up to 2 GPUs for 6 weeks), and workshops.
- Optional add‑on: Extended labelled eval (additional 500 labelled examples) — $18,000.
- Optional add‑on: Air‑gapped on‑prem appliance with onsite support (2 days) — $12,000 travel + $10,000 appliance packaging fee.
- Optional add‑on: Compliance readout + gap analysis for SOC2 readiness — $25,000.

Pricing notes and burn assumptions:
- The fixed fee covers up to 6 SEs/weeks equivalent. Any requested scope beyond the defined deliverables will be billed at standard SE day rates (TBD in master SOW).
- GPU resources for the POC are included as specified; if the customer requests larger scale testing (more GPUs or extended duration), Redwood will provide a revised estimate.

Risks & mitigation plan:
- Risk: Customer labelled set does not represent production diversity (overfitting to examples). Mitigation: we’ll reserve 20% of the budgeted eval runs for out‑of‑sample testing and propose active labelling cycles in the workshop.
- Risk: Latency SLO not met on customer network. Mitigation: test both VPC‑peered and bare‑metal on‑prem options early; optimize batching settings and reduce model context.
- Risk: High false positive rate for niche vulnerability patterns. Mitigation: create classifier cascades and conservative confidence thresholds; surface uncertain finds for manual review.

Technical approach summary:
- Use lightweight open models with quantized weights for initial runs to reduce GPU memory and speed inference.
- Pipeline: static code parser -> contract AST + heuristic feature extractor -> model inference (structured JSON output) -> postprocessor to generate suggested test harnesses.
- Caching: use prefix/KV caching for repeated contract templates and function signatures to lower per‑token costs across large corpora.

Workshop agenda (sample 2 hours):
- 00:00–00:15: Introductions, goals recap, success criteria review.
- 00:15–00:45: Demo: sample contract run, model output, ticket creation flow.
- 00:45–01:10: Metrics walk through (precision/recall, latency distribution, cost estimates).
- 01:10–01:35: Ops & security: deployment architecture, keys, logging, and access controls.
- 01:35–02:00: Roadmap & next steps: production rollout options (hosted vs dedicated vs private), pricing model, and responsibilities.

Acceptance criteria for the POC:
- SCAA deployed in customer environment accessible to designated stakeholders.
- Evaluation report shows meeting at least two of the three target success metrics (time reduction, precision threshold, private deploy checklist).
- Integration connector creates tickets in the customer system with correct structure for 90% of sample runs.

Roles and responsibilities (summary):
- Redwood SE (owner: Ethan Morales): lead integration, model selection, and evaluation report.
- Customer Sec Eng lead: provide data, approve redaction policy, validate acceptance metrics.
- Solutions Architect (Priya Nair): architecture design, deployment automation, and KMS integration.
- Customer PM: prioritize which contracts to include and schedule reviewers for the workshop.

Next steps (if approved):
1) Confirm scope & sign POC SOW addendum (this draft) within 7 business days.
2) Schedule kickoff and dataset delivery window.
3) Provision trial environment and assign SEs.

Notes to reviewers (internal):
- This pricing is intentionally conservative to allow room for additional labeling work; we should be prepared to flex the appliance/on‑site days depending on the customer’s compliance posture.
- If they ask for full production SLA during the POC, escalate to enterprise sales for a dedicated capacity quote (separate contract).

Unresolved questions for the customer (ask during kickoff):
- Do you have any locked contracts that cannot be shared even in redacted form?
- Which ticket fields are required by your workflow (priority mapping, CWE mapping, developer assignment)?
- Are there any third‑party model restrictions (e.g., cannot run models with non‑commercial licenses)?

Document history:
- 2025‑08‑07: initial draft (Ethan Morales).
- 2025‑09‑02: added detailed pricing and optional appliances (Priya Nair).
- 2026‑01‑18: internal review edits and updated evaluation targets (Liam Chen).

jake: Quick pre-release check — planning to publish v1.14.0 tomorrow morning (UTC). Need someone to push an annotated+signed tag, create a GitHub draft release, and confirm artifacts + checksums are uploaded. Leaving a short checklist below.

mina: I can take the tag + create the draft. What should the exact tag message and procedures be?

jake: Tag message: "Release v1.14.0 — runtime + CLI: perf improvements, bugfixes, changelog entries". Steps I recommend:

```
# ensure branch is up to date
git checkout release/v1.14
git pull --ff-only origin release/v1.14

# create an annotated tag
git tag -a v1.14.0 -m "Release v1.14.0 — runtime + CLI: perf improvements, bugfixes"

# (optional) GPG-sign the tag locally
git tag -s v1.14.0 -m "Release v1.14.0"

# push the tag to origin
git push origin v1.14.0
```

Then create a GitHub draft release (gh CLI):
```
# create draft with changelog as notes
gh release create v1.14.0 dist/* --notes-file CHANGELOG.md --draft
```

Artifact steps (build pipeline has produced dist/*):
```
# checksums

evidence.title: Customer Story Industry Tagging Guidelines (Sales Enablement)
evidence.text:
## Purpose
To make it possible to report on and compare customer stories, all published customer story assets must use consistent industry tags and publication markers.

## Scope
Applies to:
- Confluence case studies in: sales-enablement/case-studies/
- Google Drive one-pagers in: shared_drives/go-to-market/customer-stories/

## Required markers (for reporting)
Every published customer story must include:
- `published`
- A quarter marker like `q4-2025`
- Exactly one industry marker like `industry-fintech`

## Allowed industry segments (choose exactly one)
- `industry-fintech`
- `industry-healthcare`
- `industry-ecommerce`
- `industry-legal`
- `industry-saas`
- `industry-industrial`
- `industry-media`

## Definition: Published
"Published" means the asset is approved for external sharing by Marketing or Sales Enablement. Drafts and internal-only narratives should not carry the `published` marker.

## Common mistakes
- Multiple industry tags on one asset (not allowed)
- Missing quarter marker
- Using non-standard industries (example: `industry-banking` instead of `industry-fintech`)

evidence.title: Add “Case Studies” section to docs site nav + landing page
evidence.text:
## Context
Marketing is launching the customer reference program and needs public-facing case studies that are easy to discover and easy for Sales to link. Today, customer stories live as ad-hoc blog posts and drafts in Drive; we need a stable home in the docs site with a top-level nav entry.

This ticket covers:
1) Adding a “Case Studies” link to the docs site navigation (desktop + mobile).
2) Adding a Case Studies landing page with a reusable layout that can list current stories and future placeholders.

Non-goals (for this ticket): authoring the story content itself, publishing gated PDFs, or building a CMS workflow. We’ll keep it static (MD/MDX + frontmatter) and iterate.

## Requirements
### Functional
- Add “Case Studies” to the primary docs navigation.
- Landing page at `/case-studies` (and included in sitemap).
- Page should support:
  - Title + short intro copy
  - Card/list layout for stories (logo, summary, deployment mode, primary proof points)
  - Standard metrics disclaimer component (to support ranges / caveats)
  - Placeholder entries allowed (hidden from nav list if not ready)

### UX/IA
- “Case Studies” should live alongside other top-level resources (e.g., Docs / SDKs / Pricing links). Placement: after “Docs” and before “Changelog” (per Marketing request).
- Mobile nav and search should be consistent.

### Analytics (nice-to-have)
- Track a page view event for `/case-studies` and outbound clicks to individual stories (if we already have a click-tracking pattern).

## Acceptance Criteria
- [x] Top-level nav includes “Case Studies” linking to `/case-studies`.
- [x] Nav renders correctly on desktop and mobile; no overflow/regression at common breakpoints.
- [x] `/case-studies` page exists, builds in CI, and is linked from the nav.
- [x] Landing page includes a standardized metrics disclaimer block with approved language.
- [x] At least one placeholder entry exists so the layout is validated, even if no stories are published yet.
- [x] Docs search index includes the landing page (if search runs on our static build).
- [x] No broken links; lighthouse/build checks pass.

## Implementation Notes
- Prefer keeping the story cards data-driven via frontmatter (title, slug, deployment mode tags, summary, optional logo asset path).
- Keep the UI components minimal and reusable for future stories.
- Ensure the page works for both light/dark themes.

## Links
- Design spec: DES-611 (Customer story page layout and components)
- Program workflow context: PM-1847 (Customer reference program operational workflow)
- Docs PR (landing page + template): https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-docs/pull/4821
- Docs PR (publish first story + metrics disclaimer): https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-docs/pull/4879

## Rollout
- Land nav + landing page behind the standard docs deploy process (no feature flags).
- Coordinate publish timing with Marketing (Camila / Soojin) to ensure the nav link isn’t pointing to an empty page for more than a few days.

## Risks / Considerations
- Legal prefers metrics to be ranges in some cases; metrics disclaimer needs to be consistent across pages.
- SEO: make sure we don’t create duplicate content vs any blog post versions.
- Asset hosting for logos/diagrams should use existing docs static asset pipeline; avoid linking to Drive.

---
## Activity / Comments

### 2025-10-02 (Simran Kaur)
Picked up. Skimmed DES-611—agree with card-based layout and a reusable “proof points + disclaimer” block. Will implement landing page + components first, then nav entry.

### 2025-10-07 (Simran Kaur)
Opened PR #4821 with:
- `/case-studies` landing page scaffold
- `CaseStudyCard` component
- initial placeholder entry + frontmatter schema
Pending: nav entry placement + final copy from Marketing.

### 2025-10-09 (Soojin Lee)
Copy feedback (in PR): intro should emphasize production economics + deployment flexibility; avoid sounding like a generic “customers” page.
Also requested we include “Dedicated / Private / Hosted” tag styling.

### 2025-10-11 (Markus Klein)
Reviewed component props: please keep the tags and stats optional so we can publish stories without exact metrics. Also ensure the architecture diagram block can be inserted on individual story pages later.

### 2025-10-16 (Simran Kaur)
Addressed review notes in #4821:
- Tags optional
- Added disclaimer component hook + styling
- Updated intro copy based on Soojin’s edits

### 2025-10-21 (Camila Reyes)
Request: nav should go live only once the first story is ready. OK to merge landing page PR now; nav entry can merge after story PR is approved.

### 2025-10-28 (Simran Kaur)
Merged #4821. Created follow-up commit for nav entry (small diff) but holding merge until story is approved.

### 2025-11-04 (Simran Kaur)
PR #4879 opened by DevEx with Northwind story content + standardized metrics disclaimer language. I’ll piggyback nav entry change into that PR to keep timing aligned.

### 2025-11-06 (Simran Kaur)
Merged #4879 with nav entry + first published story. Verified on prod:
- Nav link appears in desktop + mobile
- `/case-studies` renders and lists Northwind story card
- Build checks green; no 404s
Marking ENG-9401 Done.

## Follow-ups (not in scope)
- Add click-tracking for card clicks once we confirm the analytics pattern for docs.
- Add “Case Studies” to docs site search facets (if we add facets at all).
- Consider `/customers` redirect to `/case-studies` if Marketing wants a shorter alias.

description:
Summary: Introduces a new /case-studies landing page in the docs site, adds a reusable Customer Story template component set (quote callouts, architecture diagram block, metrics disclaimer slot), and wires the section into the docs navigation. This PR also adds placeholder entries for upcoming stories so Sales/CS can link to stable URLs during the reference program ramp. Motivation: Marketing is standing up a customer reference + case study program for Dedicated/Private; we need a consistent, developer-first story format and a discoverable landing page that can scale beyond the first 2–3 stories. Scope: (1) New landing page with cards + filters (Deployment: Hosted/Dedicated/Private; Pillar: performance economics/reliability/deployment flexibility/ops tooling).
